Unlike intent, motive is usually not an essential [[Element (criminal law)|element]] of a crime: it plays various roles in investigative considerations but is normally not required to establish the defendant's guilt.<ref>{{multiref |1={{harvnb|Dubber|Hörnle|2014|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=rogfAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA239 239–240]}} |2={{harvnb|Fay|2017|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=FzYlDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA85 85–86]}} |3={{harvnb|Ormerod|Smith|Hogan|2011|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=ocGcAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA117 117]}} |4={{harvnb|Hall|2022|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=koBOEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA56 56]}} }}</ref>

In a different sense, motivation also plays a role in justifying why convicted offenders should be punished. According to the [[deterrence theory]] of law, one key aspect of punishment for law violation is to motivate both the convicted individual and potential future wrongdoers to not engage in similar criminal behavior.<ref>{{multiref |1={{harvnb|Drumbl|2007|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=t17icd-sA4cC&pg=PA169 169]}} |2={{harvnb|Siegel|Welsh|2014|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=ROTKAgAAQBAJ&pg=PT146 146]}} }}</ref>

=== Others ===
Motivation is a central factor in implementing and maintaining lifestyle changes in the fields of [[personal development]] and health.<ref>{{harvnb|Thygerson|2018|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=T5hIDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA36 36]}}</ref> Personal development is a process of self-improvement aimed at enhancing one's skills, knowledge, talents, and overall well-being. It is realized through practices that promote growth and improve different areas in one's life. Motivation is pivotal in engaging in these practices. It is especially relevant to ensure long-term commitment and to follow through with one's plans.<ref>{{multiref |1={{harvnb|Issar|Navon|2016|pp=[https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-319-20699-8_25 111–112]|loc=Personal Development}} |2={{harvnb|APA staff}} |3={{harvnb|Antoniuk|Soltyk|Chopyk|Pavlyuk|2019|pp=129–130, 136|loc=Motivation To Self-Improvement Among Physical Education Teachers}} |4={{harvnb|Thygerson|2018|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=T5hIDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA36 36]}} }}</ref> For example, health-related lifestyle changes may at times require high willpower and self-control to implement meaningful adjustments while resisting impulses and bad habits. This is the case when trying to resist urges to smoke, consume alcohol, and eat fattening food.<ref>{{multiref |1={{harvnb|Rippe|2019|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=UQqWDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA1211 1211]}} |2={{harvnb|Thygerson|2018|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=T5hIDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA36 36]}} |3={{harvnb|Fuchs|2008|p=967|loc=Motivation}} }}</ref>

Motivation plays a key role in economics since it is what drives individuals and organizations to make economic decisions and engage in economic activities. It affects diverse processes involving consumer behavior, labor supply, and investment decisions. For example, [[rational choice theory]], a fundamental theory in economics, postulates that individuals are motivated by self-interest and aim to maximize their utility, which guides [[economic behavior]] like consumption choices.<ref>{{multiref |1={{harvnb|Bronk|2009|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=RbRK-htDuv0C&pg=PA234 234]}} |2={{harvnb|Baddeley|2017|pp=8–9|loc=2. Motivation and incentives}} |3={{harvnb|Crimmins|2017|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=fQVpDQAAQBAJ&pg=PA453 453]}} |4={{harvnb|Gerhart|2017|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=eAGqDQAAQBAJ&pg=PA101 101]|loc=[https://books.google.com/books?id=eAGqDQAAQBAJ&pg=PA101 Incentives and Pay for Performance in the Workplace]}} |5={{harvnb|Zhao|2006|pp=[https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1057/9781403984623_5 52–53]|loc=Economic Motivation and Its Relevance for Business Ethics}} }}</ref>

In [[video games]], player motivation is what drives people to play a game and engage with its contents. Player motivation often revolves around completing certain [[Quest (video games)|objectives]], like solving a puzzle, beating an enemy, or exploring the game world. It concerns both smaller objectives within a part of the game as well as finishing the game as a whole.<ref>{{multiref |1={{harvnb|Pedersen|2009|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=s13Cjz_bGkgC&pg=PA75 75]}} |2={{harvnb|Pulsipher|2012|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=SkAJt4gdgwoC&pg=PA138 138]}} |3={{harvnb|Thompson|Berbank-Green|Cusworth|2007|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=Zyh4HXuHTPMC&pg=PA62 62–63]}} }}</ref> Understanding different types of player motivation helps game designers make their games immersive and appealing to a wide audience.<ref>{{multiref |1={{harvnb|Salmond|2017|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=Q3Q4DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA72 72–73]}} |2={{harvnb|Thompson|Berbank-Green|Cusworth|2007|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=Zyh4HXuHTPMC&pg=PA62 62–63]}} }}</ref>

Motivation is also relevant in the field of politics. This is true specifically for democracies to ensure active engagement, participation, and [[voting]].<ref>{{harvnb|Colby|Beaumont|Ehrlich|Corngold|2010|pp=[https://books.google.com/books?id=AGe6iRZLWg0C&pg=PA139 139–140]}}</ref>

The '''Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia – People's Army''' ({{langx|es|link=no|Fuerzas Armadas Revolucionarias de Colombia{{snd}}Ejército del Pueblo}}, '''FARC–EP''' or '''FARC''') was a far-left<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Walsh |first=Bryan |date=2016-09-12 |title=How Peace-Finally-Came to Reign Throughout the Western Hemisphere |url=https://time.com/4475617/how-peace-finally-came-to-reign-throughout-the-western-hemisphere/ |access-date=2025-06-28 |magazine=TIME |language=en |archive-date=2 November 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241102160224/https://time.com/4475617/how-peace-finally-came-to-reign-throughout-the-western-hemisphere/ |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Aidi |first=Hisham |title=Why Colombians opposed the peace deal with FARC |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2016/10/4/why-colombians-opposed-the-peace-deal-with-farc |access-date=2025-06-28 |website=Al Jazeera |language=en}}</ref> [[Marxist–Leninist]] [[Guerrilla warfare|guerrilla group]]<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-latin-america-11400950 |title=Profiles: Colombia's armed groups |work=BBC News |access-date=17 December 2014 |date=2013-08-29 |archive-date=9 December 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141209100126/http://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-latin-america-11400950 |url-status=live }}</ref> involved in the continuing [[Colombian conflict]] starting in 1964. The FARC–EP was officially founded in 1966 from peasant self-defense groups formed from 1948 during ''[[La Violencia]]'' as a peasant force promoting a political line of [[agrarianism]] and [[anti-imperialism]]. They were known to employ a variety of [[military tactics]],<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nctc.gov/site/groups/farc.html |title=Terrorist Groups: Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) |work=[[National Counterterrorism Center]] |access-date=17 December 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140712155620/http://www.nctc.gov/site/groups/farc.html |archive-date=12 July 2014}}</ref> in addition to more unconventional methods, including [[terrorism]].<ref name="inside-colombia-180">{{cite book |first=Grace |last=Livingstone |year=2004 |title=Inside Colombia: Drugs, Democracy, and War |publisher=Rutgers University Press |isbn=978-0-8135-3443-5 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cOU0bvG8ZGwC&q=farc+colombia+founded&pg=PA180 |page=180}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |doi=10.1016/S0030-4387(02)00108-4 |title=Terrorism After the Cold War: Trends and Challenges |journal=[[Orbis (journal)|Orbis]] |volume=46 |issue=2 |pages=275–287 |year=2002 |last1=Radu |first1=Michael}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=Latin America: Regions and People |first=Robert B. |last=Kent |location=New York |publisher=The Guilford Press |date=2006 |isbn=978-1-57230-909-8 |page=141}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=Organized Crime: From Trafficking to Terrorism |first1=Frank G. |last1=Shanty |first2=Patit Paban |last2=Mishra |year=2008 |location=Santa Barbara |publisher=ABC-Clio |isbn=978-1-57607-337-7 |page=323}}</ref>

The operations of the FARC–EP were funded by [[kidnap]] and [[ransom]], [[illegal mining|mining]],<ref>{{Cite news |title=Colombia army raids illegal mines funding FARC rebels |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-colombia-mining-illegal-idUSKBN0NW27220150511 |work=Reuters |date=2015-05-11 |access-date=2016-02-08 |archive-date=17 June 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170617073146/http://www.reuters.com/article/us-colombia-mining-illegal-idUSKBN0NW27220150511 |url-status=live }}</ref> [[extortion]], and taxation of various forms of economic activity, and the production and distribution of [[illegal drugs|drugs]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=McDermott |first=Jeremy |date=17 June 2012 |title=Gold overtakes drugs as source of Colombia rebel funds |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-latin-america-18396920 |access-date=21 June 2018 |archive-date=27 October 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181027194052/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-latin-america-18396920 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.economist.com/the-americas/2011/01/27/guerrilla-miners |newspaper=The Economist |title=Guerrilla miners |date=27 January 2011 |access-date=11 October 2020 |archive-date=12 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201012140356/https://www.economist.com/the-americas/2011/01/27/guerrilla-miners |url-status=live }}</ref> They are only one actor in a complex conflict where atrocities have been committed by the state, right-wing paramilitaries, and left-wing guerrillas not limited to FARC, such as ELN, M-19, and others. Colombia's [[National Centre for Historical Memory]], a government agency, has estimated that between 1981 and 2012 [[Right-wing paramilitarism in Colombia|paramilitary]] groups have caused 38.4% of the civilian deaths, while the Guerillas are responsible for 16.8%, the Colombian Security Forces for 10.1%, and other non-identified armed groups for 27.7%.<ref name=":4">{{cite web|title=Basta Ya! Memoria de Guerra y Dignidad|url=http://centrodememoriahistorica.gov.co/descargas/informes2013/bastaYa/capitulos/basta-ya-cap1_30-109.pdf|work=[[Centro Nacional De Memoria Historica]]|access-date=1 February 2022|archive-date=24 January 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220124162213/http://centrodememoriahistorica.gov.co/descargas/informes2013/bastaYa/capitulos/basta-ya-cap1_30-109.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> The National Centre for Historical Memory has also concluded that of the 27,023 kidnappings carried out between 1970 and 2010, the Guerillas were responsible for 90.6% of them.<ref name=":4"/>

The strength of the FARC–EP forces was high; in 2007, the FARC said they were an armed force of 18,000 men and women; in 2010, the Colombian military calculated that FARC forces consisted of about 13,800 members, 50 percent of whom were armed guerrilla combatants; and in 2011 the president of Colombia, [[Juan Manuel Santos]], said that FARC–EP forces comprised fewer than 10,000 members. The Colombian Ministry of Defense reported 19,504 [[deserters]], or individually demobilized members, from the FARC between August 2002 and their collective demobilization in 2017,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Nussio |first1=Enzo |last2=Ugarriza |first2=Juan E. |title=Why Rebels Stop Fighting: Organizational Decline and Desertion in Colombia's Insurgency |journal=International Security |date=2021 |volume=45 |issue=4 |pages=167–203 |doi=10.1162/isec_a_00406 |issn=0162-2889 |url=https://direct.mit.edu/isec/article/45/4/167/100570/Why-Rebels-Stop-Fighting-Organizational-Decline |doi-access=free |hdl=20.500.11850/480000 |hdl-access=free |access-date=27 April 2021 |archive-date=24 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220924115727/https://direct.mit.edu/isec/article/45/4/167/100570/Why-Rebels-Stop-Fighting-Organizational-Decline |url-status=live }}</ref> despite potentially severe punishment, including execution, for attempted desertion in the FARC.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Aguilera |first1=Mario |title=Las guerrillas marxistas y la pena de muerte a combatientes |journal=Anuario Colombiano de Historia Social y de la Cultura |date=2014 |volume=41 |issue=1 |pages=201–236 |doi=10.15446/achsc.v41n1.44855 |issn=0120-2456|doi-access=free}}</ref>

FARC made 239 attacks on the energy infrastructure; however, they showed signs of fatigue. By 2014, the FARC were not seeking to engage in outright combat with the army, instead concentrating on small-scale ambushes against isolated army units. Meanwhile, from 2008 to 2017, the FARC opted to attack police patrols with home-made mortars, sniper rifles, and explosives, as they were not considered strong enough to engage police units directly. This followed the trend of the 1990s during the strengthening of [[Military Forces of Colombia|Colombian government forces]].<ref name="caracol.com.co">{{cite web |url=http://www.caracol.com.co/noticias/actualidad/farc-cambiaron-secuestro-por-extorsion-y-se-freno-la-desmovilizacion/20131119/nota/2019212.aspx |title=Informe del Centro de Memoria Histórica conocido por Caracol Radio revela historia de las FARC de los últimos 65 años |work=[[Caracol Radio]] |language=es |access-date=1 November 2013 |date=2013-11-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131203003202/http://www.caracol.com.co/noticias/actualidad/farc-cambiaron-secuestro-por-extorsion-y-se-freno-la-desmovilizacion/20131119/nota/2019212.aspx |archive-date=3 December 2013 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

In June 2016, the FARC signed a ceasefire accord with President Santos in [[Havana]]. This accord was seen as an historic step to ending the war that has gone on for fifty years.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Brodinsky |first1=Sybilla |last2=Watts |first2=Jonathan |title=Colombia and FARC rebels sign historic ceasefire deal to end 50-year conflict |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2016/jun/23/colombia-farc-rebel-ceasefire-agreement-havana |access-date=23 June 2016 |work=[[The Guardian]] |date=23 June 2016 |archive-date=24 June 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160624120025/https://www.theguardian.com/world/2016/jun/23/colombia-farc-rebel-ceasefire-agreement-havana |url-status=live }}</ref> Santos announced that four years of negotiation had secured a [[Colombian peace process|peace deal with FARC]] and that a [[2016 Colombian peace agreement referendum|national referendum]] to ratify the deal would take place on 2 October.<ref>{{cite news |last=Brodzinsky |first=Sibylla |date=25 August 2016 |title=FARC peace deal: rebels and Colombian government sign accord to end war |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2016/aug/24/colombia-government-farc-rebels-peace-deal-52-year-war |newspaper=The Guardian |access-date=18 May 2020}}</ref> The referendum failed with 50.24% voting against.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-latin-america-37537252 |title=Colombia referendum: Voters reject FARC peace deal |work=BBC News |date=2016-10-03 |access-date=21 June 2018 |archive-date=30 September 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180930152644/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-latin-america-37537252 |url-status=live }}</ref> In November 2016, the Colombian government and the FARC signed a revised peace deal,<ref name="bbc.com">{{cite news |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-latin-america-38096179 |title=Colombia signs new peace deal with FARC |date=24 November 2016 |work=[[BBC News]] |access-date=21 June 2018 |archive-date=28 December 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161228195756/http://www.bbc.com/news/world-latin-america-38096179 |url-status=live }}</ref> which was approved by [[Congress of Colombia|Congress]].<ref name ="congress approves"/>

On 27 June 2017, FARC ceased to be an armed group, disarming itself and handing over its weapons to the [[United Nations]]. A month later, FARC announced its reformation as a legal political party, later renamed the [[Commons (Colombian political party)|Commons]], in accordance with the terms of the peace deal.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-colombia-peace-politics/after-decades-of-war-colombias-farc-rebels-debut-political-party-idUSKCN1B705U |title=After decades of war, Colombia's FARC rebels debut political party |work=Reuters |date=27 June 2017 |access-date=4 September 2017 |archive-date=5 September 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170905053931/http://www.reuters.com/article/us-colombia-peace-politics/after-decades-of-war-colombias-farc-rebels-debut-political-party-idUSKCN1B705U |url-status=live }}</ref> However, about 2,000 to 2,500 [[FARC dissidents]] still take on FARC's original doctrine and continue with drug trafficking, though far smaller than the group at its peak.<ref name="REUTperu18">{{cite news |title=Peru arrests more than 50 in anti-drug bust at Colombian border |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-peru-colombia-drug-trafficking/peru-arrests-more-than-50-in-anti-drug-bust-at-colombian-border-idUSKBN1K704T |access-date=18 July 2018 |work=[[Reuters]] |date=16 July 2018 |archive-date=17 July 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180717223931/https://www.reuters.com/article/us-peru-colombia-drug-trafficking/peru-arrests-more-than-50-in-anti-drug-bust-at-colombian-border-idUSKBN1K704T |url-status=live }}</ref>

A small faction of FARC leaders announced a return to armed activity on 29 August 2019, stating that the Colombian government did not respect peace agreements, a position Colombian officials disagreed with.<ref name=WPaug2019>{{Cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/the_americas/as-colombia-peace-accord-unravels-ex-farc-leaders-take-up-arms-to-resume-struggle/2019/08/29/e2a50bd6-ca5d-11e9-9615-8f1a32962e04_story.html |title=As Colombia peace accord unravels, ex-FARC leaders take up arms, announce return to conflict |last1=Baddour |first1=Dylan |last2=Faiola |first2=Anthony |date=29 August 2019 |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |access-date=2 September 2019 |archive-date=1 September 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190901083255/https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/the_americas/as-colombia-peace-accord-unravels-ex-farc-leaders-take-up-arms-to-resume-struggle/2019/08/29/e2a50bd6-ca5d-11e9-9615-8f1a32962e04_story.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2019/aug/29/ex-farc-rebels-announce-offensive-despite-peace-deal-colombia-video |title=Former FARC commanders say they are returning to war despite 2016 peace deal |last=Daniels |first=Joe Parkin |date=29 August 2019 |work=The Guardian |access-date=31 August 2019 |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> The Colombian government responded with preemptive strikes, killing FARC members planning to lead rearmament activities.<ref name=":2"/> In October 2023, the Colombian government engaged in peace talks with the FARC splinter group and agreed to a ceasefire. In January, both sides agreed to extend the ceasefire to June 2024.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-01-15 |title=Colombia extends cease-fire with FARC splinter group in bid to reduce rural violence |url=https://apnews.com/article/colombia-farc-emc-ceasefire-peace-talks-bogota-d09c6d3ee05e781367a124f962e5c8d8 |access-date=2024-03-02 |website=AP News |language=en |archive-date=2 March 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240302103358/https://apnews.com/article/colombia-farc-emc-ceasefire-peace-talks-bogota-d09c6d3ee05e781367a124f962e5c8d8 |url-status=live }}</ref>

As of February 2024, the vast majority of former FARC members have honored the 2016 peace agreement.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The rise of FARC dissidents: Continuation of the Colombian Crisis post-2016 Peace Deal |url=https://www.orfonline.org/expert-speak/the-rise-of-farc-dissidents-continuation-of-the-colombian-crisis-post-2016-peace-deal |access-date=2024-03-02 |website=orfonline.org |language=en |archive-date=2 March 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240302103857/https://www.orfonline.org/expert-speak/the-rise-of-farc-dissidents-continuation-of-the-colombian-crisis-post-2016-peace-deal |url-status=live }}</ref> However, in August 2024 the government announced an end to a ceasefire with the smaller dissident FARC faction the Estado Mayor Central, EMC, who reject the 2016 peace deal.<ref>{{Cite web | title=Colombia Armed Forces Restart Military Operations Against ELN Rebels | url=https://www.usnews.com/news/world/articles/2024-08-05/colombia-armed-forces-restart-military-operations-against-eln-rebels-defense-minister | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240807011642/https://www.usnews.com/news/world/articles/2024-08-05/colombia-armed-forces-restart-military-operations-against-eln-rebels-defense-minister | access-date=2025-02-22 | archive-date=2024-08-07}}</ref> In October 2024, the EMC agreed to a new ceasefire with the government.<ref>{{Cite web |author=Nick |date=2024-10-25 |title=Ceasefire extension among core points agreed in government and EMC peace talks |url=https://justiceforcolombia.org/ceasefire-extension-among-core-points-agreed-in-government-and-emc-peace-talks/ |access-date=2026-01-07 |website=justice for colombia |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Background ==
{{Main|History of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia}}
{{Further|Colombian conflict|Plan Colombia}}

=== ''La Violencia'' and the National Front ===
{{Main|La Violencia|History of Colombia#The National Front regime (1958–1974)}}
{{Quote box|align=right|width=25%|quote="There is more [[Political repression|repression]] of individual freedom here, than in any country we've been to; the police patrol the streets, carrying rifles, and demand your papers every few minutes&nbsp;... the atmosphere, here, is tense, and it seems a revolution may be brewing. The countryside is in open revolt, and the army is powerless to suppress it."|source= Diary of [[Ernesto "Che" Guevara]], 6 July 1952<ref name="che-moto-157">{{cite book |title=The Motorcycle Diaries: Notes on a Latin American Journey |url=https://archive.org/details/isbn_9781920888107 |url-access=registration |first=Ernesto "Che" |last=Guevara |publisher=Ocean Press |year=2004 |page=[https://archive.org/details/isbn_9781920888107/page/157 157]|isbn=9781920888107}}</ref>}}

In 1948, in the aftermath of the [[assassination]] of the [[populist]] politician [[Jorge Eliécer Gaitán]], a decade of large-scale political violence erupted throughout Colombia. This unrest eventually culminated in a Conservative–Liberal [[civil war]], killing more than 200,000 people. In Colombian history and culture, the killings are known as ''[[La Violencia]]'' (The Violence, 1948–58); most of the people killed were [[peasant]]s and laborers in rural Colombia.<ref name="richani-systems-23-28">{{cite book |title=Systems of Violence: the political economy of war and peace in Colombia |first=Nazih |last=Richani |location=Albany, New York |publisher=SUNY Press |year=2002 |pages=23–28 |isbn=978-0-79145-345-2}}</ref> In 1957–1958, the political leadership of the Liberal Party and the Conservative Party agreed to establish a bipartisan political system known as the [[National Front (Colombia)|National Front]] (Frente Nacional, 1958–74). The Liberal and the Conservative parties agreed to alternate in the exercise of government power by presenting a joint National Front candidate to each election and restricting the participation of other political movements.

The pact was ratified as a constitutional amendment by a national [[plebiscite]] on 1 December 1957 and was supported by the Church as well as Colombia's business leaders. The initial power-sharing agreement was effective until 1974; nonetheless, with modifications, the Liberal–Conservative bipartisan system lasted until 1990.<ref name="beyond-bogota-timeline">{{cite book |title=Beyond Bogota: Diary of a Drug War Journalist |url=https://archive.org/details/beyondbogotadiar00leec |url-access=registration |first=Garry |last=Leech |publisher=Beacon Press |location=Boston, MA |year=2009 |isbn=978-0-8070-6148-0 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/beyondbogotadiar00leec/page/242 242]–247}}</ref><ref name="evil-hour-51-52">{{cite book |first=Forrest |last=Hylton |title=Evil Hour in Colombia |publisher=Verso |year=2006 |isbn=978-1-84467-551-7 |url=https://archive.org/details/evilhourincolomb00hylt |url-access=registration |pages=[https://archive.org/details/evilhourincolomb00hylt/page/51 51]–52}}</ref> The 16-year extension of the bipartisan power-sharing agreement permitted the Liberal and Conservative elites to consolidate their socioeconomic control of Colombian society, and to strengthen the military to suppress political reform and [[radical politics]] proposing alternative forms of government for Colombia.<ref name="other-war-68">{{cite book |last=Stokes |first=Doug |title=America's Other War: Terrorizing Colombia |url=https://archive.org/details/americasotherwar00stok |url-access=limited |year=2005 |publisher=Zed Books |isbn=978-1-84277-547-9 |page=[https://archive.org/details/americasotherwar00stok/page/n88 68]}}</ref><ref name="aviles-global-32">{{cite book |title=Global Capitalism, Democracy, and Civil-Military Relations in Colombia |first=William |last=Avilés |publisher=SUNY Press |year=2006 |isbn=978-0-7914-6699-5 |page=32}}</ref><ref name="evil-hour-55-56">{{cite book |first=Forrest |last=Hylton |title=Evil Hour in Colombia |publisher=Verso |year=2006 |isbn=978-1-84467-551-7 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/evilhourincolomb00hylt/page/53 53], 55–56 |url=https://archive.org/details/evilhourincolomb00hylt|url-access=registration}}</ref>

=== Accelerated Economic Development ===
During the 1960s, the Colombian government effected a policy of Accelerated Economic Development (AED), the [[agribusiness]] plan of [[Lauchlin Currie]], a Canadian-born U.S. economist who owned ranching land in Colombia. The plan promoted [[industrial farm]]ing that would produce great yields of agricultural and animal products for worldwide exportation, while the Colombian government would provide subsidies to large-scale [[Private sector|private]] farms. The AED policy came at the expense of the small-scale family farms that only yielded food supplies for local consumption. Based on a [[Legalism (Western philosophy)|legalistic]] interpretation of what constituted "efficient use" of the land, thousands of peasants were forcefully evicted from their farms and migrated to the cities, where they became part of the industrial labor pool. In 1961, the dispossession of farmland had produced 40,000 landless families and by 1969 their numbers amounted to 400,000 throughout Colombia.<ref>{{cite book |title=Colombia: Inside the Labyrinth |url=https://archive.org/details/colombiainsidela00pear |url-access=registration |first=Jenny |last=Pearce |year=1990 |publisher=Latin American Bureau |page=[https://archive.org/details/colombiainsidela00pear/page/92 92]|isbn=9780906156445}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=Guerrilla Movements in Latin America |url=https://archive.org/details/guerrillamovemen0000unse |url-access=registration |first=Richard |last=Gott |publisher=Nelson |year=1970 |page=516|isbn=9780171380385}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=Revolution Next Door: Latin America in the 1970s |url=https://archive.org/details/revolutionnextdo0000mace |url-access=registration |first=Gary |last=MacEoin |publisher=Holt, Rinehart & Winston |year=1971 |page=[https://archive.org/details/revolutionnextdo0000mace/page/91 91]|isbn=9780030860027}}</ref> By 1970, the ''[[Latifundium|latifundio]]'' type of industrial farm (more than 50 hectares) occupied more than 77 per cent of arable land in the country.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Imperialist capitalism in the Third World: theory and evidence from Colombia |first=Raúl A. |last=Fernández |journal=Latin American Perspectives |volume=6 |issue=1 |year=1979 |page=56|doi=10.1177/0094582X7900600103 |s2cid=153927518}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=The Rape of the Peasantry: Latin America's Landholding System |first=Ernest |last=Feder |publisher=Anchor |location=New York |year=1971 |page=244}}</ref> The AED policy increased the concentration of land ownership among cattle ranchers and urban industrialists, whose businesses expanded their profits as a result of reductions in the cost of labor wages after the influx of thousands of displaced peasants into the cities.<ref name="rev-social-6-7">{{cite book |title=Revolutionary Social Change in Colombia: The Origin and Direction of the FARC-EP |first=James J. |last=Brittain |publisher=Pluto Press |year=2010 |isbn=978-0-7453-2876-8 |pages=6–7}}</ref> During this period, most rural workers lacked basic medical care and [[malnutrition]] was almost universal, which increased the rates of preventable disease and infant mortality.<ref name="rev-social-74-76">{{cite book |title=Revolutionary Social Change in Colombia: The Origin and Direction of the FARC-EP |first=James J. |last=Brittain |publisher=Pluto Press |year=2010 |isbn=978-0-7453-2876-8 |pages=74–76}}</ref>

== History ==
=== PCC and self-defense communities ===
{{Main|Marquetalia Republic}}
Communists were active throughout rural and urban Colombia in the period immediately following [[World War I]].<ref name="decker-duran-80-81">{{cite book |title=The Political, Economic, and Labor Climate in Colombia |first1=David R. |last1=Decker |first2=Ignacio |last2=Duran |publisher=University of Pennsylvania |year=1982 |pages=80–81}}</ref> The [[Colombian Communist Party]] (''Partido Comunista Colombiano'', PCC) was formally accredited by the [[Comintern]] in 1930. The PCC began establishing "peasant leagues" in rural areas and "popular fronts" in urban areas, calling for improved living and working conditions, education, and rights for the working class. These groups began networking together to present a defensive front against the state-supported violence of large landholders.<ref name="gomez-perspectives-248">{{cite book |last=Gomez |first=Alberto |date=1972 |chapter=Perspectives of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) |title=National Liberation Fronts 1960/1970: Essays, documents, interviews |location=New York |publisher=William Morrow & Company |isbn=978-0-688-02189-4 |page=248}}</ref><ref name="rev-social-2-3">{{cite book |title=Revolutionary Social Change in Colombia: The Origin and Direction of the FARC-EP |first=James J. |last=Brittain |publisher=Pluto Press |year=2010 |isbn=978-0-7453-2876-8 |pages=2–3}}</ref> Members organized strikes, protests, seizures of land, and organized communist-controlled "self-defense communities" in southern Colombia that were able to resist state military forces, while providing for the subsistence needs of the populace.<ref name="rev-social-2-3"/> Many of the PCC's attempts at organizing peasants were met with violent repression by the Colombian government and the landowning class.<ref name="rev-social-6-7"/> U.S. military intelligence estimated that in 1962, the size of the PCC had grown to 8,000 to 10,000 active members, and an additional 28,000 supporters.<ref name="bandits"/>

In 1961, a guerrilla leader and long-time PCC organizer named [[Manuel Marulanda Vélez]] declared an independent "Republic of Marquetalia". The Lleras government attempted unsuccessfully to attack the communities to drive out the guerrillas, due to fears that "a Cuban-style [[revolutionary situation]] might develop". After the failed attacks, several army outposts were set up in the area.<ref>{{cite journal |first=Dennis M. |last=Rempe |date=Winter 1995 |title=Guerrillas, Bandits, and Independent Republics: US Counter-insurgency Efforts in Colombia 1959–1965 |url=http://www.icdc.com/~paulwolf/colombia/smallwars.htm |url-status=dead |journal=Small Wars and Insurgencies |volume=6 |issue=3 |pages=304–327 |doi=10.1080/09592319508423115 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100330101500/http://www.icdc.com/~paulwolf/colombia/smallwars.htm |archive-date=30 March 2010 |access-date=13 August 2010 |quote=This was the case in 1961, when the Republic of Marquetalia was declared by guerrilla leader Manuel Marulanda Velez (also known as 'Tiro Fijo' or Sure Shot). The Lleras government, fearing that a Cuban-style revolutionary situation might develop, launched a surprise attack against the area in early 1962. Although unsuccessful in driving the irregular forces from their stronghold, several army outposts were established in the area.|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In October 1959, the United States sent a "Special Survey Team" composed of [[counterinsurgency]] experts to investigate Colombia's internal security situation. Among other policy recommendations the U.S. team advised that "to shield the interests of both Colombian and US authorities against 'interventionist' charges any special aid given for internal security was to be sterile and covert in nature".<ref name="bandits">{{cite journal |first=Dennis M. |last=Rempe |title=Guerrillas, Bandits, and Independent Republics: US Counter-insurgency Efforts in Colombia 1959–1965 |journal=Small Wars and Insurgencies |volume=6 |issue=3 |date=Winter 1995 |pages=304–327 |url=http://www.icdc.com/~paulwolf/colombia/smallwars.htm |doi=10.1080/09592319508423115 |access-date=13 August 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100330101500/http://www.icdc.com/~paulwolf/colombia/smallwars.htm |archive-date=30 March 2010|url-access=subscription }}</ref> In February 1962, three years after the 1959 "US Special Survey Team", a Fort Bragg top-level U.S. Special Warfare team headed by Special Warfare Center commander General [[William P. Yarborough]], visited Colombia for a second survey.<ref name="inside-colombia-155">{{cite book |first=Grace |last=Livingstone |year=2004 |title=Inside Colombia: Drugs, Democracy, and War |publisher=Rutgers University Press |isbn=978-0-8135-3443-5 |page=155}}</ref>

In a secret supplement to his report to the [[Joint Chiefs of Staff]], Yarborough encouraged the creation and deployment of a US-backed force to commit "[[paramilitary]], [[sabotage]] and/or [[terrorism|terrorist]] activities against known communist proponents".<ref>Visit to Colombia, South America, by a Team from Special Warfare Center, Fort Bragg, North Carolina, Headquarters, U.S. Army Special Warfare School, 26 February 1962, Kennedy Library, Box 319, National Security Files, Special Group; Fort Bragg Team; Visit to Colombia; 3/62, "Secret Supplement, Colombian Survey Report."</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=Rogue States: The Rule of Force in World Affairs |first=Noam |last=Chomsky |publisher=South End Press |year=2000 |isbn=978-0-89608-611-1 |page=[https://archive.org/details/roguestatesruleo00chom_0/page/69 69] |url=https://archive.org/details/roguestatesruleo00chom_0 |url-access=registration}}</ref><ref name="hrw-redes">{{cite web |url=https://www.hrw.org/spanish/informes/1996/colombia2.html |title=Las Redes de Asesinos de Colombia: La asociación militar-paramilitares y Estados Unidos |date=November 1996 |website=Human Rights Watch |language=es |access-date=18 May 2020 |archive-date=18 September 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100918100852/http://www.hrw.org/spanish/informes/1996/colombia2.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

The new counter-insurgency policy was instituted as [[Plan Lazo]] in 1962 and called for [https://luisvillamarin.com/obras/conflicto-colombiano/1676-Plan%20Lazo%20Estrategia%20para%20erradicar%20la%20violencia%20tripartidista%20en%20Colombia%20(1962-1965) both military operations] and [[civic action program]]s in violent areas. Following Yarborough's recommendations, the Colombian military recruited civilians into "civil defense" groups which worked alongside the military in its counter-insurgency campaign, as well as in civilian intelligence networks to gather information on guerrilla activity.<ref name="bandits"/><ref name="hrw-redes"/><ref name="other-war-71-72">{{cite book |last=Stokes |first=Doug |title=America's Other War: Terrorizing Colombia |url=https://archive.org/details/americasotherwar00stok |url-access=limited |year=2005 |publisher=Zed Books |isbn=978-1-84277-547-9 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/americasotherwar00stok/page/n91 71]–72}}</ref> [[Doug Stokes]] argues that it was not until the early part of the 1980s that the Colombian government attempted to move away from the counterinsurgency strategy represented by Plan Lazo and Yarborough's 1962 recommendations.<ref name="other-war-74">{{cite book |last=Stokes |first=Doug |title=America's Other War: Terrorizing Colombia |url=https://archive.org/details/americasotherwar00stok |url-access=limited |year=2005 |publisher=Zed Books |isbn=978-1-84277-547-9 |page=[https://archive.org/details/americasotherwar00stok/page/n94 74]}}</ref>

=== Creation of FARC ===
The Colombian government began attacking many of the communist groups in the early 1960s, attempting to re-assimilate the territories under the control of the national government. FARC was formed in 1964 by [[Manuel Marulanda Vélez]] and other PCC members, after a military [[Operation Marquetalia|attack on the community of Marquetalia]]. 16,000 Colombian troops attacked the community, which only had 48 armed fighters. Marulanda and 47 others fought against government forces at Marquetalia and then escaped into the mountains along with the other fighters. These 48 men formed the core of FARC, which later grew in size to hundreds of fighters.<ref name="lat-Amer-problems-404">{{cite book |title=Latin America, its problems and its promise: a multidisciplinary introduction |first=Jan Kippers |last=Black |publisher=Westview Press |year=2005 |isbn=978-0-8133-4164-4 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5v1gkSLNEA4C&pg=PA404 |page=404}}</ref><ref name="republics">{{cite book |first1=Jorge Pablo |last1=Osterling |first2=Xavier |last2=Sanin |title=Democracy in Colombia: Clientelist Politics and Guerrilla Warfare |publisher=Transaction Publishers |year=1989 |page=280}}</ref>

=== Betancur and Barco presidencies (1982–1990) ===
==== Seventh Guerrilla Conference of the FARC–EP ====
{{Main|Seventh Guerrilla Conference of the FARC-EP}}
In 1982, FARC–EP held its Seventh Guerrilla Conference, which called for a major shift in FARC's strategy. FARC had historically been doing most of its fighting in rural areas and was limited to small-scale confrontations with Colombian military forces. By 1982, increased income from the "coca boom" allowed them to expand into an irregular army, which would then stage large-scale attacks on Colombian troops. They also began sending fighters to Vietnam and the Soviet Union for advanced military training. They also planned to move closer to middle-sized cities, as opposed to only remote rural areas, and closer to areas rich in natural resources, in order to create a strong economic infrastructure. It was also at this conference that FARC added the initials "EP", for "''Ejército del Pueblo''" or "People's Army", to the organization's name.<ref name="walking-ghosts-47-60">{{cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/walkingghostsmur00dudl |url-access=registration |title=Walking Ghosts: Murder and Guerrilla Politics in Colombia |last=Dudley |first=Steven |date=January 2004 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-93303-2 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/walkingghostsmur00dudl/page/47 47]–56, 59–60}}</ref><ref name="human-cond-74-76">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7KLx_Po4LUMC&q=farc+tax&pg=PA74 |title=The Human Condition |first=Robert C. |last=Neville |publisher=SUNY Press |year=2001 |isbn=978-0-7914-4779-6 |pages=74–76}}</ref>

==== ''La Uribe'' Agreement and ''Union Patriótica'' ====
In the early 1980s, President [[Belisario Betancur]] began discussing the possibility of peace talks with the guerrillas. This resulted in the 1984 ''La Uribe'' Agreement, which called for a [[cease-fire]], which ended up lasting from 1984 to 1987.<ref name="voting-amid-153-154">{{cite book |title=Voting amid violence: electoral democracy in Colombia |first=Steven Lynn |last=Taylor |publisher=Northeastern University Press (UPNE) |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-55553-698-5 |pages=153–154 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xr_7dHPt9pAC&pg=PA153}}</ref>

In 1985, members of the FARC–EP, along with a large number of other leftist and communist groups, formed a political party known as the ''[[Patriotic Union (Colombia)|Union Patriótica]]'' ("Patriotic Union", UP). The UP sought political reforms (known as ''Apertura Democratica'') such as [[constitutional reform]], more democratic local elections, political decentralization, and ending the domination of Colombian politics by the Liberal and Conservative parties. They also pursued socioeconomic reforms such [[land reforms|land redistribution]], greater health and education spending, the [[nationalization]] of foreign businesses, Colombian banks, and transportation, and greater [[media democracy|public access to mass media]]. While many members of the UP were involved with the FARC–EP, the large majority of them were not and came from a wide variety of backgrounds such as [[labor unions]] and socialist parties such as the PCC.<ref name="rev-social-206-210">{{cite book |title=Revolutionary Social Change in Colombia: The Origin and Direction of the FARC-EP |first=James J. |last=Brittain |publisher=Pluto Press |year=2010 |isbn=978-0-7453-2876-8 |pages=206–210}}</ref> In the cities, the FARC–EP began integrating itself with the UP and forming ''Juntas Patrióticas'' (or "solidarity cells")—small groups of people associated with labor unions, student activist groups, and peasant leagues, who traveled into the ''barrios'' discussing social problems, building support for the UP, and determining the sociopolitical stance of the urban peasantry.<ref name="voting-amid-153-154"/><ref name="inside-insurgency-98-99">{{cite book |title=Inside insurgency: violence, civilians, and revolutionary group behavior |first=Claire |last=Metelits |publisher=NYU Press |year=2009 |isbn=978-0-8147-9578-1 |pages=98–99 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CrskYcO58oIC&pg=PA98}}</ref>

The UP performed better in elections than any other leftist party in Colombia's history. In 1986, UP candidates won 350 local council seats, 23 deputy positions in departmental assemblies, 9 seats in the House, and 6 seats in the Senate. The 1986 presidential candidate, [[Jaime Pardo Leal]], won 4.6% of the national vote.<ref name="voting-amid-153-154"/><ref name="inside-insurgency-98-99"/><ref>{{cite book |title=The Politics and Ideology of the Colombian Peasant Movement: The Case of ANUC (National Association of Peasant Smallholders) |first=Silvia Rivera |last=Cusicanqui |publisher=UN Research Institute for Social Development/CINEP |year=1987 |page=129}}</ref>

Since 1986, thousands of members of the UP and other leftist parties were murdered (estimates range from 4,000 to 6,000). In 1987, the President of the UP, Jaime Pardo, was murdered. In 1989 a single large landholder had over 400 UP members murdered. Over 70% of all Colombian presidential candidates in 1990—and 100% of those from center-left parties—were assassinated.<ref name="rev-social-206-210"/><ref name="inside-insurgency-98-99"/><ref>{{cite book |title=Our Guerrillas, Our Sidewalks: a journey into the violence of Colombia |url=https://archive.org/details/ourguerrillasour0000unse |url-access=registration |edition=2nd |first=Herbert T. |last=Braun |publisher=Rowman & Littlefield |year=2003 |page=[https://archive.org/details/ourguerrillasour0000unse/page/232 232]}}</ref><ref>For a wide-ranging survey of the violence against the UP, see also {{cite book |first=Luis Alberto Matta |last=Aldana |title=Poder Capitalista y Violencia Política en Colombia: Terrorismo de estado y genocidio contra la Unión Patriótica |publisher=Ideas y Soluciones Graficas |year=2002 |language=es}}</ref>

=== Gaviria and Samper presidencies (1990–1998) ===
During this period, the Colombian government continued its negotiations with the FARC–EP and other armed groups, some of which were successful. Some of the groups which demobilized at this time include the [[Popular Liberation Army (Colombia)|EPL]], the [[People's Revolutionary Army (Colombia)|ERP]], the Quintín Lame Armed Movement, and the [[19th of April Movement|M-19]].

On 10 August 1990, senior leader Jacobo Arenas, an ideological leader and founder of FARC–EP, died of a heart attack at the Casa Verde compound in Colombia's eastern mountains.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://global.factiva.com/ha/default.aspx#./!?&_suid=148607078504103122423171888461 |title=Veteran Colombian Guerrilla Leader Dies of Heart Attack |last=Croft |first=Adrian |date=14 August 1990 |work=Reuters News |access-date=2 February 2017 |via=Factiva |archive-date=1 March 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170301095010/http://global.factiva.com/ha/default.aspx#./!?&_suid=148607078504103122423171888461 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Towards the end of 1990, the Colombian army, with no advance warning and while negotiations were still ongoing with the group, attacked and seized four linked bases. The last of these a compound known as Casa Verde, which housed the National Secretariat of the FARC–EP, was seized on 15 December 1990.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://global.factiva.com/ha/default.aspx#./!?&_suid=148607078504103122423171888461 |title=Colombian Army Captures Houses of Guerrilla Leaders |date=16 December 1990 |work=Reuters News |access-date=2 February 2017 |via=Factiva |archive-date=1 March 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170301095010/http://global.factiva.com/ha/default.aspx#./!?&_suid=148607078504103122423171888461 |url-status=live }}</ref> The Colombian government argued that the attack was caused by the FARC–EP's lack of commitment to the process, demonstrated by continuing its criminal activities<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://global.factiva.com/ha/default.aspx#./!?&_suid=148607078504103122423171888461 |title=Colombia Presses Drive on Rebels, Smashing Base |last=Brooke |first=James |date=14 December 1990 |work=The New York Times |access-date=2 February 2017 |via=Factiva |archive-date=1 March 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170301095010/http://global.factiva.com/ha/default.aspx#./!?&_suid=148607078504103122423171888461 |url-status=live }}</ref> and FARC attacks in November.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://global.factiva.com/ha/default.aspx#./!?&_suid=148607078504103122423171888461 |title=Colombian Army Strikes Guerrillas A Blow |date=15 November 1990 |work=Reuters News |access-date=2 February 2017 |via=Factiva |archive-date=1 March 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170301095010/http://global.factiva.com/ha/default.aspx#./!?&_suid=148607078504103122423171888461 |url-status=live }}</ref>

On 3 June 1991, dialogue resumed between the [[Simón Bolívar Guerrilla Coordinating Board]] and the government on neutral territory in [[Caracas]], Venezuela and [[Tlaxcala]], Mexico.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/spanish/specials/1441_farc/page8.shtml |title=40 años de las FARC: Otros acercamientos |work=BBC Mundo |language=es}}</ref> However, the war did not stop, and armed attacks by both sides continued. The negotiation process was broken off in 1993 after no agreement was reached. The Coordinating Board disappeared not long after that time, and guerrilla groups continued their activities independently.

Before the break off of dialogue, a letter written by a group of Colombian intellectuals (among whom were [[List of Nobel laureates|Nobel laureate]] [[Gabriel García Márquez]]) to the Simón Bolívar Guerrilla Coordinating Board was released denouncing the approach taken by the FARC–EP and the dire consequences that it was having for the country.<ref>{{cite journal |url=http://www.nuso.org/upload/articulos/2246_1.pdf |title=Carta de los intelectuales colombianos a la Coordinadora Guerrilla Simón Bolívar |journal=Nueva Sociedad |number=125 |date=May–June 1993 |language=es |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090121055909/http://www.nuso.org/upload/articulos/2246_1.pdf |archive-date=21 January 2009}}</ref>

In the early 1990s, the FARC–EP had between 7,000 and 10,000 fighters, organized into 70 fronts spread throughout the country.{{Citation needed|date=September 2009}} From 1996 to 1998 they inflicted a series of strikes on the Colombian Army, including a three-day offensive in [[Mitú]] ([[Vaupés Department|Vaupés department]]), taking a large number of soldiers prisoner.

On 23 September 1994, the FARC kidnapped American agricultural scientist [[Thomas Hargrove]] and held him captive for 11 months. After his release, Hargrove wrote a book about his ordeal which inspired the 2000 film ''[[Proof of Life]]'' starring [[Meg Ryan]] and [[Russell Crowe]].

Over this period in Colombia, the cultivation of different drugs expanded and there were widespread coca farmers' marches. These marches brought to a halt several major arteries in southern Colombia. Government officials said that FARC–EP had forced the protesters to participate.<ref name="Cocalero96Ramirez">{{cite web |url=http://www.ces.fe.uc.pt/emancipa/research/en/ft/marchas.html |title=The Politics of Recognition and Citizenship in Putumayo and in the Baja Bota of Cauca: The Case of the 1996 cocalero movement |first=María Clemencia |last=Ramírez |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150923201953/http://www.ces.fe.uc.pt/emancipa/research/en/ft/marchas.html |archive-date=23 September 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |url=http://www.uasb.edu.ec/padh/revista11/actualidad/milson%20betancourt.htm |title=El movimiento de campesinos cocaleros del Putumayo en Colombia |first=Milson Betancourt |last=Santiago |date=11 October 2004 |journal=Aportes Andinos |language=es |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120311043855/http://www.uasb.edu.ec/padh/revista11/actualidad/milson%20betancourt.htm |archive-date=11 March 2012}}</ref> According to social anthropologist María Clemencia Ramírez, the relationship between the guerrillas and the marches was ambivalent: FARC–EP promoted the 1996 protests as part of their [[participatory democracy]] policies yet also exercised [[authoritarianism]], which led to tensions and negotiations with peasant leaders, but the ''[[cocalero]]'' movement brought proposals on behalf of the coca growers and defended its own interests.<ref name="Cocalero96Ramirez"/>

French sociologist Alain Labrousse, who has conducted extensive research on the illicit narcotics industry in Latin America and Central Asia, has noted similarities in the reliance on the drug trade by both the FARC–EP and the [[Taliban]]. In his thesis, Labrousse asserts that the FARC–EP leadership, like that of the Taliban, explicitly bans the use of drugs by its membership and within the local population, but vigorously advocates for legalization of drug trafficking as a tool to finance its military objectives. In both cases, the insurgency groups manage to garner significant political support of farmers who serve to benefit from the illicit drug trade, prompting grassroots mobilization, political activism, and agitation to demand legalization by the government.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Labrousse |first=Alain |date=Winter 2005 |journal=Journal of Drug Issues |volume=35 |issue=1 |pages=169–184 |doi=10.1177/002204260503500108 |title=The FARC and the Taliban's Connection to Drugs|s2cid=71937978}}</ref>

=== Pastrana presidency (1998–2002) ===
In March 1999 members of a local FARC contingent killed three United States–based indigenous rights activists, who were working with the U'Wa people to build a school for U'Wa children, and were fighting against encroachment of U'Wa territory by multinational oil corporations. The killings were questioned by many and condemned by many others, and led the United States to increase pressure on the Pastrana administration to crack down on FARC guerrillas.<ref name="murillo-col-us-74">{{cite book |title=Colombia and the United States: war, unrest, and destabilization |first1=Mario A. |last1=Murillo |first2=Jesús Rey |last2=Avirama |publisher=Seven Stories Press |year=2004 |isbn=978-1-58322-606-3 |url=https://archive.org/details/colombiaunitedst00muri |url-access=registration |page=[https://archive.org/details/colombiaunitedst00muri/page/74 74]}}</ref>

==== 1998–2002 peace process ====
[[File:FARC guerrillas marching during the Caguan peace talks (1998-2002).jpg|thumb|right|FARC guerrillas marching in formation during the Caguan peace talks (1998–2002)]]
{{Main|1999–2002 FARC-EP-Government peace process}}
With the hope of negotiating a peace settlement, on 7 November 1998, President [[Andrés Pastrana Arango|Andrés Pastrana]] granted FARC–EP a {{cvt|42000|km2|-2}} safe haven meant to serve as a confidence building measure, centred on the [[San Vicente del Caguán]] settlement.<ref>{{cite book |title=Debating Terrorism and Counterterrorism: Conflicting Perspectives on Causes, Contexts, and Responses |last=Gottlieb |first=Stuart |publisher=CQ Press |year=2013 |isbn=978-1-4522-2672-9 |location=Thousand Oaks, California |pages=237}}</ref>

After a series of high-profile guerrilla actions, including the hijacking of an aircraft, the attack on several small towns and cities, the arrest of the Irish [[Colombia Three]] (see below) and the alleged training of FARC–EP militants in bomb making by them, and the kidnapping of several political figures, Pastrana ended the peace talks on 21 February 2002 and ordered the armed forces to start retaking the FARC–EP controlled zone, beginning at midnight. A 48-hour respite that had been previously agreed to with the rebel group was not respected as the government argued that it had already been granted during an earlier crisis in January, when most of the more prominent FARC–EP commanders had apparently left the demilitarized zone.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/americas/1832060.stm |title=Colombian army moves against rebels |date=21 February 2002 |website=BBC News |access-date=3 November 2006 |archive-date=14 June 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060614071244/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/americas/1832060.stm |url-status=live }}</ref> Shortly after the end of talks, the FARC–EP kidnapped [[Oxygen Green Party]] presidential candidate [[Íngrid Betancourt]], who was travelling in Colombian territory. Betancourt was rescued by the Colombian government on 2 July 2008 (see Operation Jaque below).

==== The Colombia Three case ====
On 24 April 2002, the [[U.S. House of Representatives Committee on International Relations]] published the findings of its investigation into [[Provisional Irish Republican Army|IRA]] activities in Colombia. Their report alleged a longstanding connection between the IRA and FARC–EP, mentioned at least 15 IRA members who had been travelling in and out of Colombia since 1998, and estimated that the IRA had received at least $2&nbsp;million in drug proceeds for training FARC–EP members.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nationalreview.com/script/printpage.p?ref=/comment/comment-ehrenfeld082102.asp |title=IRA + PLO = Terror |first=Rachel |last=Ehrenfeld |date=21 August 2002 |work=[[National Review]] |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080325010019/http://www.nationalreview.com/script/printpage.p?ref=%2Fcomment%2Fcomment-ehrenfeld082102.asp |archive-date=25 March 2008 |access-date=21 May 2020}}</ref> The IRA/FARC–EP connection was first made public on 11 August 2001, following the arrest in [[Bogotá]] of two IRA explosives and [[urban warfare]] experts and of a representative of [[Sinn Féin]] who was known to be stationed in Cuba. Jim Monaghan, Martin McCauley and Niall Connolly (known as the [[Colombia Three]]), were arrested in Colombia in August 2001 and were accused of teaching bomb-making methods to FARC–EP.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2002/04/24/world/adams-delays-testifying-in-us-about-ira-action-in-colombia.html |title=Adams Delays Testifying in U.S. About I.R.A. Action in Colombia |date=24 April 2002 |work=The New York Times |first=Warren |last=Hoge |access-date=12 October 2026 |archive-date=14 February 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090214152317/http://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9A06E2DD163EF937A15757C0A9649C8B63 |url-status=live |author-link=Warren Hoge}}</ref>

On 15 February 2002, the Colombia Three were charged with training FARC–EP members in bomb-making in Colombia. The Colombian authorities had received satellite footage of the men with FARC–EP in an isolated jungle area, where they were thought to have spent five weeks. They could have spent up to 20 years in gaol if the allegations were proved.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2001/aug/16/colombia.northernireland?commentpage=1 |title=Arrested IRA man is Sinn Féin's fixer in Latin America |date=16 August 2001 |work=The Guardian |location=London |first=Rosie |last=Cowan |access-date=22 May 2010}}</ref>

During October 2001, a key witness in the case against the three Irish republicans disappeared. This came as Sinn Féin President [[Gerry Adams]] admitted one of the men was the party's representative in Cuba. The missing witness, a former police inspector, said he had seen Mr McCauley with FARC–EP members in 1998. Without his testimony, legal sources said the chances of convicting the three men were reduced.{{Citation needed|date=February 2010}}

They were eventually found guilty of travelling on false passports in June 2004 but were acquitted of training FARC–EP members. That decision was reversed after an appeal by the [[Attorney General of Colombia]] and they were sentenced to 17-year terms.<ref name="news.bbc.co.uk">{{cite news |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/northern_ireland/4140302.stm |title=Appeal to Ahern over republicans |date=11 August 2005 |work=BBC News |access-date=4 January 2010 |archive-date=20 September 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130920183439/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/northern_ireland/4140302.stm |url-status=live }}</ref> However, they vanished in December 2004 while on bail and returned to Ireland.<ref name="news.bbc.co.uk"/> [[Tánaiste]] [[Mary Harney]] said no deal had been done with Sinn Féin or the IRA over the three's return to Ireland adding that the Irish government would consider any request from the Colombian authorities for their [[extradition]].<ref name="news.bbc.co.uk"/> Colombian vice-president [[Francisco Santos Calderón]] did not rule out allowing them to serve their sentences in Ireland.

=== Uribe presidency (2002–2010) ===
==== 2002–2007 ====
[[File:FARC commanders during the Caguan peace talks (1998-2002).jpg|thumb|FARC commanders during the Caguan peace talks (1998–2002)]]
For most of the period between 2002 and 2005, the FARC–EP was in a strategic withdrawal due to the increasing military and [[Colombian National Police|police]] actions of new president [[Álvaro Uribe]], which led to the capture or desertion of many fighters and medium-level commanders. Uribe ran for office on an anti-FARC–EP platform and was determined to defeat FARC–EP in a bid to create "confidence" in the country.{{Citation needed|date=March 2010}} Uribe's own father had been killed by FARC–EP in an attempted kidnapping in 1983.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/americas/3214685.stm |title=Profile: Álvaro Uribe Velez |date=3 July 2008 |website=BBC News |access-date=18 May 2020 |archive-date=9 August 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200809134301/http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/world/americas/3214685.stm |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2002 and 2003, FARC broke up 10 large ranches in Meta, an eastern Colombian province, and distributed the land to local subsistence farmers.<ref name="crude-inter-124">{{cite book |title=Crude interventions: the US, oil and the new world (dis)order |first=Gary M. |last=Leech |publisher=Zed Books |year=2006 |isbn=978-1-84277-629-2 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=oVoHQTpWzUMC&q=farc+growers+peasants&pg=PA124 |page=124}}</ref>

During the first two years of the Uribe administration, several FARC–EP fronts, most notably in [[Cundinamarca Department|Cundinamarca]] and [[Antioquia Department|Antioquia]], were broken by the government's military operations.{{Citation needed|date=February 2010}}

On 5 May 2003, the FARC assassinated the governor of Antioquia, [[Guillermo Gaviria Correa]], his advisor for peace, former defence minister [[Gilberto Echeverri Mejía]], and eight soldiers. The FARC had kidnapped Mr. Gaviria and Mr. Echeverri a year earlier, when the two men were leading a march for peace from Medellín to Caicedo in Antioquia.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2003/05/06/world/rebels-execute-10-hostages-in-colombia.html |title=Rebels Execute 10 Hostages in Colombia |first=Juan |last=Forero |date=6 May 2003 |newspaper=The New York Times |access-date=18 May 2020 |archive-date=18 November 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201118011515/https://www.nytimes.com/2003/05/06/world/rebels-execute-10-hostages-in-colombia.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

On 13 July 2004, the office of [[the United Nations]]' [[High Commissioner for Human Rights]] publicly condemned the group, given evidence that FARC–EP violated article 17 of the additional [[Protocol II]] of the [[Geneva Convention]] and international humanitarian law, as a result of the 10 July massacre of seven peasants and the subsequent displacement of 80 individuals in San Carlos, Antioquia.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.hchr.org.co/publico/comunicados/2004/cp0423.pdf |title=FARC-EP violan el DIH en San Carlos, Antioquia |date=13 July 2004 |work=Oficina En Colombia Del Alto Comisionado De Las Naciones Unidas Para Los Derechos Humanos |access-date=1 March 2010 |language=es |archive-date=21 September 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090921222925/http://www.hchr.org.co/publico/comunicados/2004/cp0423.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In early February 2005, a series of small-scale actions by the FARC–EP around the southwestern departments of Colombia, resulted in an estimated 40 casualties. The FARC–EP, in response to government military operations in the south and in the southeast, displaced its [[center of gravity (military)|military centre of gravity]] towards the [[Nariño Department|Nariño]], [[Putumayo Department|Putumayo]] and [[Cauca Department|Cauca]] departments.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/world/americas/4252071.stm |title='Deadliest' hit on Colombian army |date=10 February 2005 |website=BBC News |access-date=5 November 2006 |archive-date=26 February 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080226221023/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/americas/4252071.stm |url-status=live }}</ref>

The FARC–EP originally said that they would only release the police and military members they held captive (whom they considered to be prisoners of war) through exchanges with the government for imprisoned FARC–EP members.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.cambio.com.co/portadacambio/841/ARTICULO-WEB-NOTA_INTERIOR_CAMBIO-5836431.html |title=Habla 'Cano' |work=[[Cambio (magazine)|Cambio]] |access-date=17 October 2011 |language=es |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120216090131/http://www.cambio.com.co/portadacambio/841/ARTICULO-WEB-NOTA_INTERIOR_CAMBIO-5836431.html |archive-date=16 February 2012}}</ref> During the duration of the [[demilitarised zone|DMZ]] negotiations, a small humanitarian exchange took place.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://colombiajournal.org/colombia70.htm |title=Prisoner Release Represents FARC's First Political Concession |work=Colombia Journal |first=Martin |last=Dayani |date=2 July 2001 |access-date=14 October 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130524004133/http://colombiajournal.org/colombia70.htm |archive-date=24 May 2013 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

The group demanded a demilitarized zone including two towns (Florida and Pradera) in the strategic region of Valle del Cauca, where much of the current military action against them has taken place. This region is also an important way of transporting drugs to the Pacific coast and was even the primary location for [[Norte del Valle Cartel]] and [[Cali Cartel]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Bargent |first=James |date=2017-03-27 |title=Valle del Cauca: A War too Far for the Gaitanistas? |url=https://insightcrime.org/news/analysis/valle-del-cauca-a-war-too-far-for-the-urabenos/ |access-date=2023-06-29 |website=InSight Crime |language=en-US |archive-date=29 June 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230629190511/https://insightcrime.org/news/analysis/valle-del-cauca-a-war-too-far-for-the-urabenos/ |url-status=live }}</ref> This demand was rejected by the Colombian government based on previous experience during the 2002 peace talks.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.wilsoncenter.org/sites/default/files/media/documents/publication/Peace.Conflict.English.pdf|title=CUADERNOS DEL CONFLICTO PEACE INITIATIVES AND COLOMBIA ́S ARMED CONFLICT}}</ref>

On 2 December 2004, the government announced the pardon of 23 FARC–EP prisoners, to encourage a reciprocal move. The prisoners to be released were all of low rank and had promised not to rejoin the armed struggle. In November 2004, the FARC–EP had rejected a proposal to hand over 59 of its captives in exchange for 50 guerrillas imprisoned by the government.<ref name=Release>{{cite web |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/americas/4063797.stm |title=Colombia 'to release FARC rebels' |date=2 December 2006 |website=BBC News |access-date=5 November 2006 |archive-date=26 February 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080226224523/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/americas/4063797.stm |url-status=live }}</ref>

In a communique dated 28 November but released publicly on 3 December, the FARC–EP declared that they were no longer insisting on the demilitarization of San Vicente del Caguán and Cartagena del Chairá as a precondition for the negotiation of the prisoner exchange, but instead that of Florida and Pradera in the [[Valle del Cauca Department|Valle]] department.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.farcep.org/novedades/comunicados/sec2004/diciembre_03.php |title=Comunicado las FARC |date=28 November 2004 |website=FARC-EP |language=es |access-date=11 November 2006 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060305112347/http://www.farcep.org/novedades/comunicados/sec2004/diciembre_03.php |archive-date=5 March 2006}}</ref> They state that this area would lie outside the "area of influence" of both their Southern and Eastern Blocks (the FARC–EP's strongest) and that of the military operations being carried out by the Uribe administration.{{citation needed|date=November 2023}}

They requested security guarantees both for the displacement of their negotiators and that of the guerrillas that would be freed, which were stated to number as many as 500 or more, and ask the Catholic Church to coordinate the participation of the United Nations and other countries in the process.{{Citation needed|date=February 2010}}

The FARC–EP also mention in the communique that [[Simón Trinidad]]'s [[extradition]], would be a serious obstacle to reaching a prisoner exchange agreement with the government.<ref name="associated20041231">{{cite news |title=Colombia extradites top rebel commander to U.S. |work=Chicago Tribune |date=31 December 2004 |first=Gary |last=Marx}}</ref> On 17 December 2004, the Colombian government authorized Trinidad's extradition to the United States, but stated that the measure could be revoked if the FARC–EP released all political hostages and military captives in its possession before 30 December. The FARC–EP rejected the demand.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2008-03-08 |title=Al Jazeera English - News - Us Court Sentences Colombian Rebel |url=http://english.aljazeera.net/NR/exeres/168ACAE6-7FFA-4DA2-8A7F-744873BB5FB2.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080308094619/http://english.aljazeera.net/NR/exeres/168ACAE6-7FFA-4DA2-8A7F-744873BB5FB2.htm |url-status=dead |archive-date=2008-03-08 |access-date=2025-04-03 }}</ref>

On 25 March 2006, after a public announcement made weeks earlier, the FARC–EP released two captured policemen at La Dorada, Putumayo. The release took place some {{convert|335|mi}} southwest of Bogotá, near the Ecuadorean border. [[International Committee of the Red Cross|The Red Cross]] said the two were released in good health. Military operations in the area and bad weather had prevented the release from occurring one week earlier.<ref>{{cite web |work=[[International Committee of the Red Cross]] |title=Colombia: two police officers released |date=25 March 2006 |url=http://www.icrc.org/web/eng/siteeng0.nsf/html/colombia-news-250306!OpenDocument |access-date=5 November 2006 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060614093237/http://www.icrc.org/web/eng/siteeng0.nsf/html/colombia-news-250306!OpenDocument |archive-date=14 June 2006}}</ref>

In a separate series of events, the German government and a foreign ministry crisis team negotiated the release of civilian hostage and German citizen Lothar Hintze on 4 April 2006 after five years in captivity. Hintze had been kidnapped from a tourist center in Prado on 16 March 2001<ref name="m468">{{cite news |last=Usi |first= Eva | title=Lothar Hintze liberado por las FARC | website=dw.com | date=2006-04-05 | url=https://www.dw.com/es/lothar-hintze-liberado-por-las-farc/a-1955838 | language=es | access-date=2024-06-10}}</ref> for extortion purposes. His wife had paid multiple ransom payments with no result.<ref name="k339">{{cite news | title=Colombia.- La esposa del alemán liberado por las FARC revela que pagó varias veces para poner fin al secuestro | publisher=Europa Press | date=2006-04-07 | url=https://www.notimerica.com/politica/noticia-colombia-esposa-aleman-liberado-farc-revela-pago-varias-veces-poner-fin-secuestro-20060407115420.html | language=es | access-date=2024-06-10}}</ref>

One prisoner, Julian Ernesto Guevara Castro, a police officer, died of tuberculosis on 28 January 2006. He was a captain and was captured on 1 November 1998.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9C03E2D8133EF935A25751C0A9609C8B63 |title=Colombia: Hostage Held Since 1998 Dies |first=Juan |last=Forero |date=16 February 2006 |newspaper=The New York Times |access-date=6 November 2006 |archive-date=13 November 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071113183038/http://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9C03E2D8133EF935A25751C0A9609C8B63 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="DailyJournal">{{cite web |url=http://www.thedailyjournalonline.com/article.asp?CategoryId=12393&ArticleId=224940 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070819030102/http://www.thedailyjournalonline.com/article.asp?CategoryId=12393&ArticleId=224940 |url-status=usurped |archive-date=19 August 2007 |title=Police officer dead as rebel captive |access-date=13 February 2008 |work=[[The Daily Journal (Venezuela)|The Daily Journal]]}}</ref> On 29 March 2009, the FARC–EP announced that they would give Guevara's remains to his mother. The FARC handed over Guevara's remains on 1 April 2010.<ref>{{cite web |agency=Associated Press |url=http://www.etaiwannews.com/etn/news_content.php?id=906674&lang=eng_news |title=Colombian rebels to turn over officer's remains |work=[[Taiwan News]] |date=30 March 2009 |access-date=17 October 2011 |archive-date=26 September 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110926213247/http://www.etaiwannews.com/etn/news_content.php?id=906674&lang=eng_news |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Another civilian hostage, [[Fernando Araújo Perdomo|Fernando Araújo]], later named Minister of Foreign Relations and formerly Development Minister, escaped his captors on 31 December 2006. Araújo had to walk through the jungle for five days before being found by troops in the hamlet of San Agustin, {{convert|350|mi}} north of Bogotá. He was kidnapped on 5 December 2000 while jogging in the Caribbean coastal city of Cartagena. He was reunited with his family on 5 January 2007.<ref name="SMH20070106">{{cite news |url=https://www.smh.com.au/news/World/Former-Colombian-minister-escapes-rebels/2007/01/06/1167777308484.html |title=Former Colombian minister escapes rebels |access-date=13 February 2008 |work=The Sydney Morning Herald |date=6 January 2007 |archive-date=4 February 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080204081614/http://www.smh.com.au/news/World/Former-Colombian-minister-escapes-rebels/2007/01/06/1167777308484.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

Another prisoner, [[Jhon Frank Pinchao|Frank Pinchao]], a police officer, escaped his captors on 28 April 2007 after nine years in captivity. He was reunited with his family on 15 May 2007.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PtNls51VBN0C&q=Jhon+Frank+Pinchao&pg=PT35 |title=Letters to My Mother: A Message of Love, A Plea for Freedom |last1=Betancourt |first1=Ingrid |last2=Delloye-Betancourt |first2=Lorenzo |last3=Delloye-Betancourt |first3=Melanie |date=2011-03-01 |publisher=Abrams |isbn=978-1-61312-033-0 |language=en}}</ref>

==== 2007 death of 11 hostage deputies ====
{{Main|Valle del Cauca Deputies hostage crisis}}
On 28 June 2007, the FARC–EP reported the death of 11 out of 12 provincial deputies from the [[Valle del Cauca Department]] whom the guerrillas had kidnapped in 2002. The guerrillas claimed that the deputies had been killed by crossfire during an attack by an "unidentified military group." The Colombian government stated that government forces had not made any rescue attempts and that the FARC–EP executed the hostages. FARC did not report any other casualties on either side and delayed months before permitting the Red Cross to recover the remains. According to the government, the guerrillas delayed turning over the corpses to let decomposition hide evidence of how they died. The Red Cross reported that the corpses had been washed and their clothing changed before burial, hiding evidence of how they were killed. The Red Cross also reported that the deputies had been killed by multiple close-range shots, many of them in the backs of the victims, and even two by shots to the head.{{Citation needed|date=September 2011}}<ref name="bbc20070628">{{cite news |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/americas/6251878.stm |title=Colombia rebels 'killed hostages' |access-date=13 February 2008 |work=BBC News |date=28 June 2007 |archive-date=22 October 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141022045039/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/americas/6251878.stm |url-status=live }}</ref>

In February 2009, Sigifredo López, the only deputy who survived and was later released by FARC, accused the group of killing the 11 captives and denied that any military rescue attempt had taken place. According to López, the unexpected arrival of another guerrilla unit resulted in confusion and paranoia, leading the rebels to kill the rest of the Valle deputies. He survived after previously being punished for insubordination and was held in chains nearby but separated from the rest of the group.<ref name="IPSLopezReveals">{{cite web |url=http://ipsnews.net/news.asp?idnews=45707 |title=Colombia: Ex-Hostage Says FARC Killed 11 Captives |access-date=6 January 2010 |work=[[Inter Press Service]] |date=2 February 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100327122628/http://www.ipsnews.net/news.asp?idnews=45707 |archive-date=27 March 2010}}</ref>

==== Early-2008 prisoner events ====
On 10 January 2008, former vice presidential candidate [[Clara Rojas]] and former congresswoman [[Consuelo González]] were freed after nearly six years in captivity.<ref name="ChinaPost20080203">{{cite web |url=http://www.chinapost.com.tw/international/2008/02/03/141735/FARC-hostages.htm |title=FARC hostages send letter to Uribe |access-date=13 February 2008 |work=The China Post |location=Taiwan (ROC) |date=3 February 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081009041649/http://www.chinapost.com.tw/international/2008/02/03/141735/FARC-hostages.htm |archive-date=9 October 2008}}</ref> In a Venezuela-brokered deal, a helicopter flew deep into Colombia to pick up both hostages. The women were escorted out of the jungle by armed guerrillas to a clearing where they were picked up by Venezuelan helicopters that bore [[International Red Cross]] insignias.<ref name="npr.org">{{cite web |url=https://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=18017068 |title=Colombian Rebels Free Two Female Hostages |first1=Renee |last1=Montagne |first2=Juan |last2=Forero |work=National Public Radio |date=11 January 2008}}</ref> In a statement published on a pro-rebel Web site, the FARC–EP said the unilateral release demonstrated the group's willingness to engage the Colombian government in talks over the release of as many as 800 people who are still being held.<ref name="npr.org"/> In a televised speech, Colombia's U.S.-allied president, [[Álvaro Uribe]], thanked Chávez for his efforts.

During the period she was held kidnapped in the jungle in 2004, Clara Rojas gave birth to her son by [[Caesarean]]. At eight months old, the baby was removed from the area and Rojas did not hear of the boy again until 31 December, when she heard Colombian President Álvaro Uribe say on the radio that the child was no longer with her captors. [[DNA]] tests later confirmed the boy, who had been living in a Bogotá [[foster home]] for more than two years under a different name, was hers. She reclaimed her son.<ref name="abcnews.go.com">{{cite web |url=https://www.abcnews.go.com/International/wireStory?id=4125500 |title=Freed Colombian Hostages Relate Ordeal |work=ABC News |date=12 January 2008 |access-date=17 April 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110629042342/http://abcnews.go.com/International/wireStory?id=4125500 |archive-date=29 June 2011 |url-status=dead}}</ref> Asked about her opinion of the FARC–EP as group, Rojas called it "a criminal organisation", condemning its kidnappings as "a total violation of human dignity" and saying some captive police and soldiers are constantly chained.<ref name="abcnews.go.com"/>

On 31 January 2008, the FARC–EP announced that they would release civilian hostages Luis Eladio Perez Bonilla, [[Gloria Polanco]], and Orlando Beltran Cuellar to Venezuelan President [[Hugo Chávez]] as a humanitarian gesture. On 27 February 2008, the three hostages and Jorge Eduardo Gechem Turbay (who was added to the list due to his poor health) were released by FARC–EP.
