The Colombian government and the FARC on 24 November signed a revised [[Colombian peace process|peace deal]],<ref name="bbc.com"/> which Congress approved on 30 November.<ref name="congress approves">{{Cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/the_americas/colombian-congress-approves-historic-peace-deal/2016/11/30/9b2fda92-b5a7-11e6-939c-91749443c5e5_story.html |title=Colombia's congress approves historic peace deal with FARC rebels |first1=Joshua |last1=Partlow |first2=Nick |last2=Miroff |date=30 November 2016 |newspaper=The Washington Post |access-date=2016-12-01 |archive-date=1 December 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161201090410/https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/the_americas/colombian-congress-approves-historic-peace-deal/2016/11/30/9b2fda92-b5a7-11e6-939c-91749443c5e5_story.html |url-status=live |name-list-style=and}}</ref>

On 18 February 2017, the last FARC guerrillas arrived in a designated transition zone, where they began the process of disarming. The rebels stayed in the zones until 31 May, after which they were registered and reintegrated into civilian life.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-latin-america-39018686 |title=Colombia's FARC rebels complete move to demobilisation zones |date=19 February 2017 |work=BBC News |access-date=19 February 2017 |archive-date=19 February 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170219055239/http://www.bbc.com/news/world-latin-america-39018686 |url-status=live }}</ref>

On 27 June 2017, the FARC ceased to be an armed group, with its forces disarming and handing more than 7,000 weapons to the [[United Nations]] at a ceremony hosted by the FARC leadership, and the Colombian government, which included the Cabinet and President [[Juan Manuel Santos]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://apnews.com/6c77aa2530ab4bc2a4863da519b308ca |title=Colombia takes big step to peace as rebels lay down guns |website=Associated Press |date=27 June 2017 |access-date=18 May 2020 |archive-date=18 June 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200618055100/https://apnews.com/6c77aa2530ab4bc2a4863da519b308ca |url-status=live }}</ref> Peace observers had received the coordinates of 873 weapons caches hidden in Colombia's remote forests and mountains. The UN was able to remove 510 of these weapons caches, leaving the remaining 363 caches for the military to pick up.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://colombiareports.com/farc-demobilization-ends-8100-arms-22000kg-explosives-removed/ |title=FARC demobilization ends: 8,100 arms and 22000kg of explosives removed |first=Adriaan |last=Alsema |date=15 August 2017 |work=Colombia Reports |access-date=15 August 2017 |archive-date=16 August 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170816000845/https://colombiareports.com/farc-demobilization-ends-8100-arms-22000kg-explosives-removed/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

The last batch of weapons belonging to former FARC rebels has been removed under UN supervision. The United Nations collected 8,112 guns, 1.3&nbsp;million bullets, 22 tons of explosives, 3,000 grenades and 1,000 land mines from the FARC.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Armario |first1=Christine |title=UN removes last container holding Colombia rebel arms |url=https://www.ctvnews.ca/world/article/un-removes-last-container-holding-colombia-rebel-arms/ |access-date=4 October 2020 |agency=Associated Press |date=15 August 2017 |language=en |archive-date=22 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220722025127/https://www.ctvnews.ca/world/un-removes-last-container-holding-colombia-rebel-arms-1.3546997 |url-status=live }}</ref>

The [[Special Jurisdiction of Peace]] (''Jurisdicción Especial para la Paz'', JEP) would be the transitional justice component of the Comprehensive System, complying with Colombia's duty to investigate, clarify, prosecute and punish serious human rights violations and grave breaches of international humanitarian law which occurred during the armed conflict. Its objectives would be to satisfy victims' right to justice, offer truth to the public, contribute to the reparation of victims, contribute to the fight against impunity, adopt decisions which give full legal security to direct and indirect participants in the conflict and contribute to the achievement of a stable and lasting peace.<ref name="abcjep">{{cite web |title=ABC Jurisdicción Especial para la Paz |url=http://www.altocomisionadoparalapaz.gov.co/Documents/informes-especiales/abc-del-proceso-de-paz/abc-jurisdiccion-especial-paz.html |work=Oficina del Alto Comisionado para la Paz |language=es |access-date=24 August 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161005125954/http://www.altocomisionadoparalapaz.gov.co/Documents/informes-especiales/abc-del-proceso-de-paz/abc-jurisdiccion-especial-paz.html |archive-date=5 October 2016 |url-status=dead}}</ref> At the end of a six-day visit to Colombia, on 9 October 2017 the UN [[Assistant Secretary-General]] for human rights Andrew Gilmour issued statement welcoming progress in the demobilization and disarmament of the FARC. However, he expressed, "concern about problems in the implementation of the accords which relate to the continued attacks against human rights defenders and community leaders."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ohchr.org/EN/NewsEvents/Pages/DisplayNews.aspx?NewsID=22215&LangID=E |title=Colombia: UN Assistant Secretary-General for Human Rights urges effective protection of rights defenders amid continued attacks |date=9 October 2017 |website=[[OHCHR]]}}</ref>

=== Duque presidency (2018–2022) ===
==== Membership in Colombian Congress ====
On 20 July 2019, ten former FARC members, including former senior leader Pablo Catatumbo, were sworn in as members of the [[Congress of Colombia]].<ref name=swornin>{{Cite web |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2018/07/colombia-swears-farc-rebels-congress-180721053449072.html |title=Ex-FARC rebels sworn into Colombia's Congress |date=21 July 2018 |website=Al Jazeera |access-date=28 December 2019 |archive-date=28 December 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191228145129/https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2018/07/colombia-swears-farc-rebels-congress-180721053449072.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=againswornin>{{Cite news |url=https://www.ft.com/content/8ab52f2a-8c77-11e8-bf9e-8771d5404543 |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20221210/https://www.ft.com/content/8ab52f2a-8c77-11e8-bf9e-8771d5404543 |archive-date=10 December 2022 |title=FARC members take seats in Colombia's congress for first time |date=21 July 2018 |work=[[Financial Times]] |url-access=subscription}}</ref> All of these ex-rebels are members of the [[Common Alternative Revolutionary Force]] political party.<ref name=swornin/><ref name=againswornin/> Five of these ten ex-FARC rebels were sworn in as members of the [[Chamber of Representatives of Colombia|House of Representatives]], while the other five were sworn in as members of the [[Senate of Colombia|Senate]].<ref name=swornin/><ref name=againswornin/> As part of the peace agreement, these ten seats will remain under control of members from the Common Alternative Revolutionary Force until 2026.<ref name=swornin/>

==== 2019: Attempt to reinstate FARC ====
[[File:Ivan-Marquez-GoraHerria.jpg|thumb|234x234px|Former second-in-command FARC leader, [[Iván Márquez]], who called for renewed actions against the Colombian government]]
In a video published on 29 August 2019, former second-in-command FARC leader Iván Márquez announced his return to arms in the name of the guerrilla movement. Márquez denounced that the Government did not comply with its part of the Havana accord, with 667 local activists and 150 former guerrillas killed since the peace accord was signed.<ref name=":1"/><ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2019/08/29/farc-leader-announces-return-war-colombia/ |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220112/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2019/08/29/farc-leader-announces-return-war-colombia/ |archive-date=12 January 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live |title=FARC leader announces return to war for Colombia |last=Alexander |first=Harriet |date=2019-08-29 |work=The Daily Telegraph |access-date=2019-08-29 |language=en-GB |issn=0307-1235}}{{cbignore}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite web |url=https://www.elmundo.es/internacional/2019/08/29/5d67e55c21efa0d3258b456f.html |title=Más del 90 por ciento de los ex guerrilleros de las FARC siguen comprometidos con el proceso de paz |date=2019-08-29 |work=[[El Mundo (Spain)|El Mundo]] |language=es |access-date=2019-09-02 |archive-date=2 September 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190902020618/https://www.elmundo.es/internacional/2019/08/29/5d67e55c21efa0d3258b456f.html |url-status=live }}</ref> This position was criticized by former FARC supreme leader [[Timoleón Jiménez|Rodrigo Londoño]], who assured that his party remains committed to peace agreements and that "[m]ore than 90 percent of former FARC guerrillas remain committed to the peace process".<ref name=":3"/> Londoño also criticized Márquez, stating that the majority of former guerrillas killed were [[FARC dissidents]] who continued armed actions.<ref name=":3"/>

After the announcement, President Iván Duque authorized the Joint Special Operations Command to start an offensive operation. Government forces conducted a bombing raid in [[San Vicente del Caguán]] in which twelve people identified as FARC dissidents were killed. According to Duque, one of them, Gildardo Cucho, was the leader of the group which would be joining Iván Márquez in the rearmament.<ref name=":2">{{Cite news |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2019/08/colombian-farc-dissidents-killed-bombing-raid-190831063910790.html |title=9 Colombian FARC dissidents killed in bombing raid |work=Al Jazeera |date=31 August 2019 |access-date=31 August 2019 |archive-date=31 August 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190831103853/https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2019/08/colombian-farc-dissidents-killed-bombing-raid-190831063910790.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.europapress.es/internacional/noticia-fuerzas-colombianas-matan-nueve-presuntos-disidentes-farc-20190830200715.html |title=Las fuerzas colombianas matan a nueve presuntos disidentes de las FARC |work=EuropaPress |date=30 August 2019 |access-date=31 August 2019 |language=es |archive-date=31 August 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190831013858/https://www.europapress.es/internacional/noticia-fuerzas-colombianas-matan-nueve-presuntos-disidentes-farc-20190830200715.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.lavanguardia.com/politica/20190831/47104049131/sube-a-12-la-cifra-de-disidentes-muertos-en-operacion-militar-en-colombia.html |title=Sube a 12 la cifra de disidentes muertos en operación militar en Colombia |date=31 August 2019 |work=[[La Vanguardia]] |access-date=31 August 2019 |language=es |archive-date=31 August 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190831210927/https://www.lavanguardia.com/politica/20190831/47104049131/sube-a-12-la-cifra-de-disidentes-muertos-en-operacion-militar-en-colombia.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Duque also accused Venezuelan president [[Nicolás Maduro]] of assisting FARC and providing a safe haven for militants in Venezuela.<ref name=WPaug2019/>

A Truth Commission report released in 2022 shows that the drug trafficking charges against [[Jesús Santrich]] and his arrest in 2019 were a plot by the [[DEA]] and Colombian Attorney General Néstor Humberto Martínez to jeopardize the peace agreement, incite the FARC to take up arms again, and send a message to the public that the peace agreement had failed.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://cambiocolombia.com/articulo/poder/la-dea-la-fiscalia-y-un-coronel-entramparon-el-proceso-de-paz |title=La DEA, la Fiscalía y un coronel entramparon el proceso de paz &#124; Cambio Colombia |date=21 August 2022 |access-date=22 August 2022 |archive-date=23 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220823233624/https://cambiocolombia.com/articulo/poder/la-dea-la-fiscalia-y-un-coronel-entramparon-el-proceso-de-paz |url-status=live }}</ref>

====2020–2021====
General Luis Fernando Navarro asserted on January 5, [[2021 in Colombia|2021]], that FARC lost 1,500 members in 2020. The number includes deaths, capture, and desertions. He said the FARC still had 2,500 armed members.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Acosta |first1=Luis Jaime |title=Colombia's illegal armed groups lost more than 5,000 members in 2020 -military commander |url=https://www.yahoo.com/news/colombias-illegal-armed-groups-lost-130359730.html |access-date=January 5, 2021 |work=news.yahoo.com |agency=Reuters |publisher=Yahoo News |date=January 5, 2021 |archive-date=7 January 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210107214940/https://www.yahoo.com/news/colombias-illegal-armed-groups-lost-130359730.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Financing ==
FARC received most of its funding—which was estimated to average some US$300&nbsp;million per year—from taxation of the [[illegal drug trade]] and other activities, ransom kidnappings, bank robberies, and extortion of large landholders, multinational corporations, and agribusiness. From taxation of illegal drugs and other economic activity,<ref name="independent.co.uk">{{cite news |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/americas/farc-rebel-group-in-peace-talks-is-colombias-50year-war-about-to-end-8722917.html |title=FARC rebel group in peace talks: Is Colombia's 50-year war about to end? |work=The Independent |access-date=17 December 2014 |date=2013-07-20 |archive-date=17 December 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141217150127/http://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/americas/farc-rebel-group-in-peace-talks-is-colombias-50year-war-about-to-end-8722917.html |url-status=live }}</ref> FARC was estimated to receive US$60–100&nbsp;million per year.<ref name="human-cond-74-76"/><ref name="inside-rebellion-291"/>

=== Means of financing ===
The guerillas's main means of financing was through the drug trade which includes both direct and indirect participation; taxation, administration or control of areas of production and trafficking. A large but often difficult to estimate portion of funding comes from the taxation of businesses and even local farmers, often lumped in with or defined by its opponents as extortion.<ref name="coha.org">{{cite web |url=http://www.coha.org/farc-%E2%80%93-rebels-with-a-cause/ |title=FARC – Rebels with a Cause? |date=6 July 2010 |work=[[Council on Hemispheric Affairs]] |access-date=17 December 2014 |archive-date=23 September 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150923205446/http://www.coha.org/farc-%E2%80%93-rebels-with-a-cause/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

==== Drug trade ====
{{Main|Illegal drug trade in Colombia}}
FARC was not initially involved in direct drug cultivation, trafficking, or trans-shipment prior to or during the 1980s. Instead, it maintained a system of taxation on the production that took place in the territories that they controlled, in exchange for protecting the growers and establishing law and order in these regions by implementing its own rules and regulations.<ref name="ferro">{{cite journal |url=http://www.mamacoca.org/feb2002/art_ferro_Farc_y_coca_Caguan_es.html |title=Las FARC y su relación con la economía de la coca en el sur de Colombia: Testimonios de Colonos y Guerrilleros |first=Juan Guillermo Ferro |last=Medina |date=March 2000 |journal=L'Ordinaire Latino-americain |number=179 |language=es |location=Toulouse, France |publisher=Institut Pluridisciplinaire pour les Études sur l'Amérique Latine à Toulouse |access-date=18 May 2020 |archive-date=15 February 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200215103606/http://www.mamacoca.org/feb2002/art_ferro_Farc_y_coca_Caguan_es.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="other-war-101-102">{{cite book |title=America's Other War: Terrorizing Colombia |first=Doug |last=Stokes |publisher=Zed Books |year=2005 |isbn=978-1-84277-547-9 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OoQSQw-v4pYC&q=farc+paramilitaries&pg=PA101 |pages=101–102}}</ref><ref name="vanguard-rev-135-137"/> During the 1990s, FARC expanded its operations, in some areas, to include trafficking and production, which had provided a significant portion of its funding.<ref name="drugs-democ-103">{{cite book |title=Drugs and Democracy in Latin America: The Impact of U.S. Policy |editor1-first=Coletta |editor1-last=Youngers |editor2-first=Eileen |editor2-last=Rosin |location=Boulder, CO |publisher=Lynne Rienner Publishers |year=2005 |isbn=978-1-58826-254-7 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jAzNQGZ0AV4C&q=farc+paramilitaries&pg=PA103 |page=103}}</ref> Right-wing paramilitary groups also receive a large portion of their income from drug trafficking and production operations.<ref name="drugs-democ-103"/>

A 1992 [[Central Intelligence Agency]] report "acknowledged that the FARC had become increasingly involved in drugs through their "taxing" of the trade in areas under their geographical control and that in some cases the insurgents protected trafficking infrastructure to further fund their insurgency",<ref name="other-war-86-87">{{cite book |last=Stokes |first=Doug |title=America's Other War: Terrorizing Colombia |url=https://archive.org/details/americasotherwar00stok |url-access=limited |year=2005 |publisher=Zed Books |isbn=978-1-84277-547-9 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/americasotherwar00stok/page/n106 86]–87}}</ref> but also described the relationship between the FARC and the drug traffickers as one "characterized by both cooperation and friction"'' and concluded that ''"we do not believe that the drug industry [in Colombia] would be substantially disrupted in the short term by attacks against guerrillas. Indeed, many traffickers would probably welcome, and even assist, increased operations against insurgents."<ref name="cia-1992">{{cite web |url=http://www.gwu.edu/~nsarchiv/NSAEBB/NSAEBB69/col24.pdf |title=Narco-Insurgent Links in the Andes |date=29 July 1992 |website=[[Central Intelligence Agency]] |via=[[National Security Archive]] |access-date=18 May 2020 |archive-date=17 June 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140617084847/http://www2.gwu.edu/~nsarchiv/NSAEBB/NSAEBB69/col24.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 1994, the [[Drug Enforcement Administration]] (DEA) came to three similar conclusions. First, that any connections between drug trafficking organizations and Colombian insurgents were "ad hoc 'alliances of convenience'".<ref name="1994-dea-report">{{cite web |url=http://www.gwu.edu/~nsarchiv/NSAEBB/NSAEBB69/col33.pdf |title=Insurgent Involvement in the Colombian Drug Trade |date=June 1994 |website=[[Drug Enforcement Administration]] |via=National Security Archive |access-date=18 May 2020 |archive-date=17 June 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140617084840/http://www2.gwu.edu/~nsarchiv/NSAEBB/NSAEBB69/col33.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> Second, that "the independent involvement of insurgents in Colombia's domestic drug productions, transportation, and distribution is limited&nbsp;... there is no evidence that the national leadership of either the FARC or the [[National Liberation Army (Colombia)|ELN]] has directed, as a matter of policy, that their respective organizations directly engage in independent illicit drug production, transportation, or distribution."<ref name="1994-dea-report"/> Third, the report determined that the DEA "has no evidence that the FARC or ELN have been involved in the transportation, distribution, or marketing of illegal drugs in the United States. Furthermore it is doubtful that either insurgent group could develop the international transportation and logistics infrastructure necessary to establish independent drug distribution in the United States or Europe&nbsp;... DEA believes that the insurgents never will be major players in Colombia's drug trade."<ref name="1994-dea-report"/>

FARC had called for crop substitution programs that would allow coca farmers to find alternative means of income and subsistence. In 1999, FARC worked with a United Nations alternative development project to enable the transition from coca production to [[Sustainable food system|sustainable food]] production. On its own, the group had also implemented [[agrarian reform]] programs in Putumayo.<ref name="other-war-101-102"/><ref name="vanguard-rev-135-137"/><ref name="murillo-col-us-93">{{cite book |title=Colombia and the United States: war, unrest, and destabilization |first1=Mario A. |last1=Murillo |first2=Jesús Rey |last2=Avirama |publisher=Seven Stories Press |year=2004 |isbn=978-1-58322-606-3 |url=https://archive.org/details/colombiaunitedst00muri |url-access=registration |page=[https://archive.org/details/colombiaunitedst00muri/page/69 69]}}</ref>

In those FARC controlled territories that do produce coca, it is generally grown by peasants on small plots; in paramilitary or government controlled areas, coca is generally grown on large plantations.<ref>{{cite book |last=Schulte-Bockholt |first=Alfredo |title=The Politics of Organized Crime and the Organized Crime of Politics: a study in criminal power |publisher=Lexington |year=2006 |page=135}}</ref> The FARC–EP generally made sure that peasant coca growers receive a much larger share of profits than the paramilitaries would give them,<ref name="inside-rebellion-291">{{cite book |title=Inside rebellion: the politics of insurgent violence |first=Jeremy M. |last=Weinstein |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2007 |isbn=978-0-521-86077-2 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=N3-pSjAWGccC&q=farc+tax&pg=PA291 |page=291}}</ref><ref name="vanguard-rev-135-137">{{cite book |title=Vanguard revolutionaries in Latin America: Peru, Colombia, Mexico |first=James Francis |last=Rochlin |publisher=Lynne Rienner Publishers |year=2003 |isbn=978-1-58826-106-9 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_vOEi4Xf5FMC&q=farc+crop+substitution&pg=PA135 |pages=135–137}}</ref><ref name="beyond-bogata-223">{{cite book |title=Beyond Bogotá: Diary of a Drug War Journalist in Colombia |first=Garry |last=Leech |publisher=Beacon Press |year=2009 |isbn=978-0-8070-6145-9 |url=https://archive.org/details/beyondbogotadiar00leec |url-access=registration |page=[https://archive.org/details/beyondbogotadiar00leec/page/223 223]}}</ref> and demanded that traffickers pay a decent wage to their workers.<ref name="inside-rebellion-291"/> When growers in a FARC-controlled area were caught selling coca to non-FARC brokers, they were generally forced to leave the region, but when growers were caught selling to FARC in paramilitary-controlled areas, they were generally killed.<ref name="beyond-bogata-223"/> Lower prices paid for raw coca in paramilitary-controlled areas lead to significantly larger profits for the drug processing and trafficking organizations, which means that they generally prefer that paramilitaries control an area rather than FARC.<ref name="beyond-bogata-223"/>

In 2000, FARC Spokesman [[Simon Trinidad]] said that taxes on drug laboratories represented an important part of the organization's income, although he did not say how much it was. He defended this funding source, arguing that drug trade was endemic in Colombia because it had pervaded many sectors of its economy.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.dominicstreatfeild.com/2010/11/26/interview-with-simon-trinidad-farc-spokesman/2/ |title=FARC guerrilla #1: Simón Trinidad, FARC Spokesman at the Negotiating Table |first=Dominic |last=Streatfeild |date=20 November 2000 |website=dominicstreatfeild.com |access-date=18 May 2020 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120312221213/http://www.dominicstreatfeild.com/2010/11/26/interview-with-simon-trinidad-farc-spokesman/2/ |archive-date=12 March 2012}}</ref>

After 21 April 2001 capture of Brazilian drug lord [[Luiz Fernando da Costa]] (a.k.a. Fernandinho Beira-Mar) in Colombia, Colombian and Brazilian authorities accused him of cooperating with FARC–EP through the exchange of weapons for cocaine. They also claimed that he received armed protection from the guerrilla group.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.emol.com/noticias/todas/detalle/detallenoticias.asp?idnoticia=185620 |title='Fernandinho Beira-Mar', un temible capo aliado de Hernández Norambuena |date=15 June 2005 |newspaper=[[El Mercurio]] |language=es |access-date=1 September 2006 |archive-date=29 May 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070529114836/http://www.emol.com/noticias/todas/detalle/detallenoticias.asp?idnoticia=185620 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.clarin.com/diario/2001/04/25/i-02801.htm |title=Un capo narco reveló lazos con poderosos de Brasil |date=25 April 2001 |newspaper=[[Clarín (Argentine newspaper)|Clarín]] |language=es |access-date=11 November 2006 |archive-date=23 May 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060523002210/http://www.clarin.com/diario/2001/04/25/i-02801.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/portuguese/noticias/2001/010422_beiramar2.shtml |title=Polícia investiga relação de Beira-Mar com as FARC |date=22 April 2001 |website=[[BBC Brasil]] |language=pt |access-date=3 November 2006 |archive-date=28 July 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200728133614/https://www.bbc.com/portuguese/noticias/2001/010422_beiramar2.shtml |url-status=dead}}</ref>

On 18 March 2002 the [[Attorney General of the United States]] [[John Ashcroft]] indicted leaders of the FARC after an 18-month investigation into their narcotics trafficking. [[Tomás Molina Caracas]], the commander of the FARC's 16th Front, led the 16th Front's drug-trafficking activities together with Carlos Bolas and a rebel known as Oscar El Negro. Between 1994 and 2001, Molina and other 16th Front members controlled Barranco Minas, where they collected cocaine from other FARC fronts to sell it to international drug traffickers for payment in currency, weapons and equipment.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.justice.gov/archive/ag/speeches/2002/031802newsconferencefarc.htm |title=#03-14-02: Attorney General Ashcroft announces indictment charging members of FARC with drug trafficking |work=U.S. Dept. of Justice |date=18 March 2002 |access-date=14 October 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.latinamericanstudies.org/drugs/farc-leaders.htm |title=FARC leaders indicted in U.S. |first=Jerry |last=Seper |date=19 March 2002 |work=The Washington Times |via=LatinAmericanStudies.org |access-date=14 October 2012 |archive-date=13 January 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120113001025/http://www.latinamericanstudies.org/drugs/farc-leaders.htm |url-status=live }}</ref>

On 22 March 2006 the Attorney General Alberto Gonzales announced the indictment of fifty leaders of FARC for exporting more than $25&nbsp;billion worth of cocaine to the United States and other countries. Several of the FARC leaders appeared on the Justice Department's Consolidated Priority Organization target list, which identifies the most dangerous international drug trafficking organizations. Recognizing the increased profits, the FARC moved to become directly involved in the manufacture and distribution of cocaine by setting the price paid for cocaine paste and transporting it to jungle laboratories under FARC control. The charged FARC leaders ordered that Colombian farmers who sold paste to non-FARC buyers would be murdered and that U.S. fumigation planes should be shot down.<ref name="justice">{{cite web |url=https://www.justice.gov/dea/pubs/pressrel/pr032206c.html |title=Transcript of Attorney General's Press Conference Announcing Charges Against 50 Leaders of Narco-Terrorist FARC in Colombia |date=22 March 2006 |work=U.S. Dept. of Justice |access-date=4 April 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140111214415/http://www.justice.gov/dea/pubs/pressrel/pr032206c.html |archive-date=11 January 2014 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.justice.gov/usao/nys/pressreleases/March06/farcindictmentpr.pdf |title=United States charges 50 leaders of Narco-Terrorist FARC in Colombia with supplying more than half of the world's cocaine |date=22 March 2006 |work=U.S. Dept. of Justice |access-date=14 October 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120122111152/http://www.justice.gov/usao/nys/pressreleases/March06/farcindictmentpr.pdf |archive-date=22 January 2012}}</ref>

On 11 October 2012 Jamal Yousef, a.k.a. "Talal Hassan Ghantou", a native of Lebanon, was sentenced to 12 years in prison for conspiring to provide military-grade weapons to the Fuerzas Armadas Revolucionarias de Colombia (the FARC), in exchange for over a ton of [[cocaine]]. Yousef pleaded guilty in May 2012 to one count of providing material support to the FARC.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.fbi.gov/newyork/press-releases/2012/lebanese-man-sentenced-to-12-years-in-prison-for-conspiring-to-provide-material-support-to-terrorists |title=Lebanese Man Sentenced to 12 Years in Prison for Conspiring to Provide Material Support to Terrorists |date=11 October 2012 |work=Federal Bureau of Investigation |access-date=14 October 2012 |archive-date=16 October 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121016050432/http://www.fbi.gov/newyork/press-releases/2012/lebanese-man-sentenced-to-12-years-in-prison-for-conspiring-to-provide-material-support-to-terrorists |url-status=live }}</ref>

==== Kidnappings ====
{{Main|Kidnappings in Colombia}}
The FARC–EP carried out both ransom and politically motivated [[kidnappings]] in Colombia and was responsible for the majority of such kidnappings carried out in the country.<ref name="KidnappingEconomy2001">{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2001/06/03/magazine/03KIDNAPPING.html |title=The Kidnapping Economy in Colombia |work=[[The New York Times]] Magazine |date=3 June 2001 |first=Kirk |last=Semple |access-date=7 February 2017 |archive-date=9 March 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160309185612/http://www.nytimes.com/2001/06/03/magazine/03KIDNAPPING.html |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="ArmedGroupExtortion2000">{{cite web |url=http://www.unhcr.org/refworld/country,,USCIS,,COL,,3ae6a6a44,0.html |title=Colombia: Kidnapping and Extortion by Armed Groups in Urban and Suburban Areas |work=[[United States Citizenship and Immigration Services|United States Bureau of Citizenship and Immigration Services]] |date=3 January 2000 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121016184309/http://www.unhcr.org/refworld/country,,USCIS,,COL,,3ae6a6a44,0.html |archive-date=16 October 2012}}</ref><ref name="AMNESTY-Report-2009">{{cite web |url=https://www.amnesty.org/en/region/colombia/report-2009 |title=Human Rights in the Republic of Colombia |work=[[Amnesty International]] |year=2009 |access-date=4 December 2016 |archive-date=26 January 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150126091642/https://www.amnesty.org/en/region/colombia/report-2009 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

The guerrillas initially targeted the families of drug traffickers, the wealthy upper-class and foreigners but the group later expanded its kidnapping and extortion operations to include the middle-class.<ref name="KidnappingEconomy2001"/><ref name="ArmedGroupExtortion2000"/><ref name="BBC-MassExodus">{{cite news |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/programmes/from_our_own_correspondent/1314619.stm |title=Colombia's mass exodus |work=BBC News |date=5 May 2001}}</ref>

During the 1984 peace negotiations, FARC pledged to stop kidnapping and condemned the practice. However, hostage-taking by FARC increased in the years following this declaration. In a 1997 interview, FARC–EP Commander [[Alfonso Cano]] argued that some guerrilla units continued to do so for "political and economic reasons" in spite of the prohibition issued by the leadership.<ref name="HRW-without-quarter">{{cite web |url=http://www.unhcr.org/refworld/docid/3ae6a7e30.html |title=War Without Quarter: Colombia and International Humanitarian Law |work=[[Human Rights Watch]] |date=1 October 1998 |access-date=7 November 2010 |archive-date=15 October 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121015045220/http://www.unhcr.org/refworld/docid/3ae6a7e30.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2000, the FARC–EP issued a directive called "Law 002" which demanded a "tax" from all individuals and corporations with assets worth at least US$1&nbsp;million, warning that those who failed to pay would be detained by the group.<ref name="KidnappingEconomy2001"/><ref name="BBC-MassExodus"/> In 2001, FARC Commander [[Simón Trinidad]] claimed that the FARC–EP does not engage in kidnapping but instead "retains [individuals] in order to obtain resources needed for our struggle". Commander Trinidad said he did not know how many people had been taken by FARC or how much money was collected by the organization in exchange for their freedom.<ref name="KidnappingEconomy2001"/> In addition, FARC spokesperson [[Joaquín Gómez (guerrilla)|Joaquín Gómez]] stated that the payment demanded was a tax which many people paid "voluntarily", with kidnapping undertaken because "those who have the resources must pay their share".<ref name="Telegraph-2001">{{cite news |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/1399580/Colombia-Factfile-Kidnap-capital-of-the-world.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220112/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/1399580/Colombia-Factfile-Kidnap-capital-of-the-world.html |archive-date=12 January 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live |title=Colombia Factfile: Kidnap capital of the world |work=The Daily Telegraph |location=London |date=28 September 2001 |first=Jeremy |last=McDermott}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

In 2002, [[Amnesty International]] sent a letter to FARC–EP Commander [[Manuel Marulanda]] condemning kidnapping and hostage-taking as well as rejecting the threats directed at municipal or judicial officials and their families, arguing that they are civilians who are protected by [[international humanitarian law]] as long as they do not participate in hostilities.<ref name="AMNESTY-Marulanda-2002">{{cite web |url=https://www.amnesty.org/en/library/info/AMR23/124/2002/en |title=Colombia: Letter for the attention of Mr Manuel Marulanda, Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia – People's Army |date=16 December 2002 |website=Amnesty International |access-date=7 October 2010 |archive-date=11 June 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110611123703/http://www.amnesty.org/en/library/info/AMR23/124/2002/en |url-status=live }}</ref>

According to [[Amnesty International]], the number of kidnappings decreased in the last years of the conflict, but the human rights organization estimated that FARC and ELN guerrillas continued to be behind hundreds of cases until their disarming.<ref name="AMNESTY-Report-2009"/> In 2008, press reports estimated that about 700 hostages continued to be held captive by FARC.<ref name="Guardian-FAQ-EndFarc">{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2008/jul/04/colombia.france |title=FAQ: Is this the end for FARC? |work=The Guardian |location=London |date=4 July 2008}}</ref><ref name="BBC-New-Kidnappings">{{cite news |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/americas/7188509.stm |title=New FARC kidnappings in Colombia |work=BBC News |date=14 January 2008 |access-date=7 November 2010 |archive-date=15 March 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100315160215/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/americas/7188509.stm |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="AlJazeera-Hostages-Arrive">{{cite web |url=http://english.aljazeera.net/news/americas/2008/02/200852513634245678.html |title=FARC hostages arrive in Venezuela |work=Al Jazeera |date=28 February 2008 |access-date=7 November 2010 |archive-date=7 February 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110207080946/http://english.aljazeera.net/news/americas/2008/02/200852513634245678.html |url-status=live }}</ref> According to the ''Fundación País Libre'' anti-kidnapping NGO, an estimated total of 6,778 people were kidnapped by FARC between 1997 and 2007.<ref name="IPS_NoImmediateEnd">{{cite web |url=http://ipsnews.net/news.asp?idnews=40631 |title=No Immediate End to Kidnap Victims' Pain |work=IPS News |date=28 December 2007 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120314051448/http://ipsnews.net/news.asp?idnews=40631 |archive-date=14 March 2012}}</ref> In 2009, the state's anti-kidnapping agency ''Fondelibertad'' reviewed 3,307 officially unsettled cases and removed those that had already been resolved or for which there was insufficient information. The agency concluded that 125 hostages remained in captivity nationwide of whom 66 were being held by the FARC–EP.<ref name="Economist-Kidnappings-2009">{{cite news |url=https://www.economist.com/the-americas/2009/04/23/how-many-hostages |title=How many hostages? More than the government claims |newspaper=The Economist |date=23 April 2009 |access-date=7 November 2010 |archive-date=23 June 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120623020446/http://www.economist.com/node/13528083?story_id=13528083 |url-status=live }}</ref> The government's revised figures were considered "absurdly low" by ''Fundación País Libre'', which has argued that its own archives suggest an estimated 1,617 people taken hostage between 2000 and 2008 remain in the hands of their captors, including hundreds seized by FARC.<ref name="Economist-Kidnappings-2009"/> FARC claimed at the time that it was holding nine people for ransom in addition to hostages kept for a prisoner exchange.<ref name="Economist-Kidnappings-2009"/>

In 2008, Venezuelan President Hugo Chávez expressed his disagreement with FARC–EP's resorting to kidnappings.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/worldNews/idUSN1336689820080113 |title=Hugo Chávez tells Colombian rebels to stop kidnapping |date=13 January 2008 |website=[[Reuters]] |access-date=23 December 2008 |archive-date=10 February 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090210042402/http://www.reuters.com/article/worldNews/idUSN1336689820080113 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="CSM_VenezuelaExtortion">{{cite web |url=https://www.csmonitor.com/World/Americas/2008/0613/p07s04-woam.html |title=FARC extortion rackets in Venezuela, say locals |work=[[The Christian Science Monitor]] |date=13 June 2008 |access-date=7 November 2010 |archive-date=10 November 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101110092543/http://www.csmonitor.com/World/Americas/2008/0613/p07s04-woam.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Former President [[Fidel Castro]] of Cuba also criticized the use of hostage-taking by the guerrillas as "objectively cruel" and suggested that the group free all of its prisoners and hostages.<ref name="BBC-FidelCastro">{{cite news |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/7492506.stm |title=Fidel Castro in FARC hostage plea |work=BBC News |date=6 July 2008}}</ref>

In February 2012, FARC announced that it would release ten members of the security forces, who it described as political prisoners, representing the last such captives in its custody. It further announced the repeal of Law 002, bringing to an end its support for the practice of kidnapping for ransom.<ref name="BBC vow">{{cite news |title=Colombia FARC rebels vow to free hostages |access-date=26 February 2012 |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-latin-america-17173832 |work=BBC News |date=26 February 2012}}</ref><ref name="Guardian captives">{{cite news |title=Colombian rebel group says it will free all captives |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2012/feb/26/colombian-rebels-to-free-captives |access-date=26 February 2012 |newspaper=The Guardian |date=26 February 2012 |location=London}}</ref> However, it was not clear from the FARC statement what would happen to the civilians it still held in captivity.<ref>{{cite news |title=La guerrilla colombiana dice que dejará de tener rehenes políticos |url=http://mexico.cnn.com/mundo/2012/02/26/las-farc-anuncian-que-dejaran-de-usar-al-secuestro-como-arma-politica |access-date=26 February 2012 |work=[[CNN en Español|CNN México]] |date=26 February 2012 |language=es |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120227044523/http://mexico.cnn.com/mundo/2012/02/26/las-farc-anuncian-que-dejaran-de-usar-al-secuestro-como-arma-politica |archive-date=27 February 2012}}</ref> Colombian president [[Juan Manuel Santos]] used Twitter to welcome the move as a "necessary, if insufficient, step in the right direction".<ref>{{cite magazine |title=Colombia's FARC Announces Kidnapping Halt |url=http://www.time.com/time/world/article/0,8599,2107664,00.html |access-date=26 February 2012 |date=26 February 2012 |magazine=TIME |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120226225033/http://www.time.com/time/world/article/0%2C8599%2C2107664%2C00.html |archive-date=26 February 2012}}</ref>

== Women in the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia ==

=== Participation and roles ===
Estimates of the number of female combatants in the FARC vary. Some sources suggest that women made up approximately 40% of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC).<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |title=Rifles And Rhinestones: The Experiences Of Female Fighters In The Colombian Guerrilla War |url=https://www.arts.kuleuven.be/mosa/blog/rifles-and-rhinestones-the-experiences-of-female-fighters-in-the-colombian-guerrilla-war |access-date=2025-04-22 |website=Faculteit Letteren |language=en}}</ref> Furthermore, between 1985 and 2012, it was estimated that over 11,000 women had been group members.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-03-20 |title=From war to economic reintegration: The challenges for women ex-combatants in Colombia |url=https://www.theigc.org/blogs/gender-equality/war-economic-reintegration-challenges-women-ex-combatants-colombia#:~:text=Over%2011,000%20women%20participated%20in,the%20FARC%20combatants%20were%20women. |access-date=2025-04-22 |website=International Growth Centre |language=en}}</ref> Other studies present lower figures. By 2000, according to Carey (2006), women made up one-third of FARC's members. Similarly, Gutíerrez Sanín (2008) found that female participation varied by unit. Female participation was approximately 30% within units attached to FARC's top leadership, likely due to the presence of [[orderlies]] and [[Secretary|secretaries]], while central operational units had less than 10% female participation. In contrast, women's participation was much higher on the more "typical" combat fronts, accounting for 19% of the unit's members.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |title=The Woman Warrior. A Post-structural Gender Analysis of Guerrilleras in Colombia {{!}} Lund University |url=https://www.lunduniversity.lu.se/lup/publication/1405316 |access-date=2025-04-22 |website=lunduniversity.lu.se}}</ref>

According to former guerrillas, FARC–EP units typically consist of one-quarter to nearly one-half women, with some even containing girls aged eight or nine. This practice is not unique to FARC; other armed groups in [[Colombia]] also recruit girls and women as combatants. Of the 112 former child [[guerillas]] interviewed by [[Human Rights Watch]], over a quarter were girls, most of whom were former members of FARC–EP.<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |title=HRW: "You'll Learn Not To Cry": Child Combatants in Colombia: 7. GIRLS |url=https://www.hrw.org/reports/2003/colombia0903/10.htm |access-date=2025-04-22 |website=hrw.org}}</ref>

Contrary to traditional gender roles, women actively engaged in combat on the frontlines alongside their male counterparts, rather than being restricted to domestic tasks such as nursing or cooking.<ref name=":5"/> They trained in weapon handling, intelligence gathering, and military operations, and, like their male colleagues, they faced the same risks of death and injury.<ref name=":7"/>

=== History of women in the FARC ===

==== Early Involvement and marginalization (1960s–1970s) ====
Women's involvement in the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) began early, with two of the group's original 48 combatants being female during the Marquetalia resistance.<ref name=":11">{{cite thesis |last=Kermanshahchi |first=Ellaheh Tamina |title=Women and FARC: Another Oppressor or an Unlikely Liberator? |date=12 June 2020 |type=BA thesis |publisher=Utrecht University |url=https://studenttheses.uu.nl/bitstream/handle/20.500.12932/39442/BA%20Thesis%20-%20Final%20Draft.pdf}}</ref> However, their roles were largely supportive rather than combat-oriented. In the 1960s, FARC operated as a peasant self-defense group primarily consisting of male combatants. Women and children were present daily but did not engage in combat or leadership roles. In fact, according to one guerrilla fighter,<blockquote>"In the 1960s, women accompanied men and participated in activities like cooking. During the Marquetalia resistance in 1964, women were helpers, they did not carry weapons. They participated actively, but were not fundamental. In the 1960s we had a mix of people... with women, children and even dogs."<ref name=":9">{{Cite journal |last1=Sanín |first1=Francisco Gutiérrez |last2=Carranza Franco |first2=Francy |date=2017 |title=Organizing women for combat: The experience of the FARC in the Colombian war |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/joac.12238 |journal=Journal of Agrarian Change |language=en |volume=17 |issue=4 |pages=770–778 |doi=10.1111/joac.12238 |bibcode=2017JAgrC..17..770S |issn=1471-0366|url-access=subscription }}</ref></blockquote>In the latter half of the 1960s, FARC transformed into a mobile guerrilla armed group from a domestic model. It became an almost all-male force; men were expected to leave behind their families to form a fully mobilized unit, while women were largely relegated to support roles like assistance and cooking.<ref name=":9"/>

FARC maintained ties with the pro-Soviet Communist Party (CP), which sought to promote female participation by creating specialized women's organizations, following a broader trend among communist movements worldwide. FARC, in tandem, also formed specialized female organizations; however, they were restricted to traditional roles such as cooking, food organization, and laundry. Neither the CP nor FARC expected women to engage in combat.<ref name=":9"/>

==== Internal debates and shifting roles (1970s–1980s) ====
As FARC expanded in the 1970s, women's involvement in the group became a topic of debate. [[Manuel Marulanda|Tirofijo]], FARC's leader at the time, originally opposed women's participation in combat, citing their physical limitations for combat and lack of resilience as concerns. However, as FARC transformed into a more structured and militaristic army, it became evident that women's roles and participation needed to expand. During FARC's 7th National Conference in 1982, women's rights were added to the force's agenda; however, it only concerned women's rights within the group rather than broader gender equality.<ref name=":11"/>

At the same time, FARC rebranded itself as the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia – People's Army (FARC–EP) and adopted a stricter hierarchical and militaristic structure. This shift emphasized strict discipline, separation from civilians, lifelong commitment, ideological instruction, continuous training, and tight control over members' personal lives. These changes stimulated a greater incentive and need to include women within its combat ranks.<ref name=":9"/>

==== Gender equality and military integration (1980s) ====
By 1985, FARC officially declared gender equality within its ranks and started actively recruiting women as combatants. The integration of women helped to reinforce the group's independence and autonomy by diminishing the effect of outside influences, as a members' entire lives—personal and professional—could exist within the confines of the organization.<ref name=":11"/>

==== FARC's 2016 declaration: women at the forefront of change ====
In 2016, FARC publicly declared to be part of a "worldwide [movement] against...patriarchy and all forms of discrimination between human beings," a stance driven mainly by women within the group.<ref name=":11"/>

=== Motivation of women for joining ===
Women and girls cite various reasons for joining FARC. The top motives include domestic or sexual abuse and an overall lack of meaningful options for women in Colombia. Oftentimes, in some regions, they will join armed groups as a way to avoid prostitution or working in cocoa production.<ref name=":10">{{Cite web |title=GovInfo |url=https://www.govinfo.gov/app/details/GOVPUB-Y3_P31-PURL-gpo148386 |access-date=2025-04-22 |website=govinfo.gov |date=January 2016 |language=en}}</ref> This is especially true for women from rural areas who are enmeshed in poverty.<ref name=":5"/> However, women do not join just to avoid plights in their regions. To them, FARC often represents a way to escape restrictive gender roles and to access educational and leadership opportunities not available to women in the broader Colombian public. For example, a female FARC commander wanted to join at age 13 to learn how to read. However, she was told she could not join until she turned 14 years old.<ref name=":10"/> Another reason that women join is to gain the opportunity to defend their political convictions, which is especially true for wealthier, more educated women. Women essentially use their limited options to be able to safeguard and champion for female social and reproductive rights.<ref name=":5"/> In addition to ideological and educational motivations, some women and girls are drawn to the power that the FARC represents. Like many male recruits, female recruits are attracted to the group's militaristic elements. They like the idea of a uniform and being able to carry a gun.<ref name=":7"/> Female combatants also often join under the impression that they will be on the same level as their male counterparts; one of the FARC's main allures is the assertion of gender equality within its ranks.<ref name=":6"/> Overall, FARC functions as a "lifeline" to many girls and women, representing a space where female combatants can find "a certain degree of autonomy and personal development," which is often inaccessible to Colombian women, especially ones from rural regions.<ref name=":11"/>

=== Gender dynamics in FARC ===

==== Daily life and gender policies ====
During its tenure, FARC officially promoted gender equality: both men and women received the same basic military training, shared living quarters, and performed equal duties in combat. Some women even wore feminine embellishments, such as jewelry, in contrast to the group's militarized masculinity.<ref name=":5"/> In regions like Putumayo, FARC installed clear behavioral rules, mediating domestic disputes and punishing gender-based violence—sometimes with severe penalties, like death. FARC formally prohibited sexual harassment and rape and, unlike some other paramilitary groups, did not systematically use sexual violence to assert territorial control.<ref name=":10"/> Despite these regulations, significant gender-based disparities persisted in practice.<ref name=":7"/>

==== Exploitation and power imbalances ====
Many women and girls faced gendered exploitation. Commanders often would use their authority to start sexual relationships with underage girls in exchange for privileges, gifts, and protection. These relationships—sometimes described as consensual—occurred in a context of a stark power imbalance, where refusal was difficult, and a female combatant's safety often depended on compliance.<ref name=":7"/> Furthermore, many female combatants reportedly faced sexual harassment or assault.<ref name=":6"/>

==== Division of labor ====
A gendered division of labor was present. While women also fought, trained, and were subject to the same rules as men, women were often relegated to traditionally feminine roles, such as nursing or radio operating.<ref name=":9"/><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Schmidt |first=Rachel |date=2021-03-08 |title=Contesting the Fighter Identity: Framing, Desertion, and Gender in Colombia |url=https://academic.oup.com/isq/article-abstract/65/1/43/5936132?redirectedFrom=fulltext |journal=International Studies Quarterly |volume=65 |issue=1 |pages=43–55 |doi=10.1093/isq/sqaa075 |issn=0020-8833|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Women in the FARC typically held the lowest positions in the groups, often carrying gear, marching, and caring for hostages. On that note, men rarely attended to hostages—this role was almost exclusively assigned to women. Overall, women were primarily foot soldiers with heavy workloads equal to the men.<ref name=":6"/>

==== Leadership and advancement ====
Opportunities for career advancement were limited. While some women led small units, only one—Elsa Nedis Mosquera, known as "Karina"—rose to the position of Front Commander. No woman reached the top decision-making body, the Secretariat.<ref name=":9"/> Male members overwhelmingly held higher leadership roles.<ref name=":8">{{Cite journal |last=Stanski |first=Keith |title=Terrorism, Gender, and Ideology: A Case Study of Women who Join the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) |url=https://cerac.org.co/assets/pdf/Stanski_Volume_I_Chapter_10.pdf |journal=The Making of a Terrorist: Recruitment |volume=I |article-number=10}}</ref> Success and survival often hinged on the sexual "services" they provided, leading many women to view their bodies as tools or weapons within the group's internal power structure.<ref name=":11"/> Some women gained influence through relationships with male leaders, receiving privileges such as better guard shifts or informal leadership roles.<ref name=":6"/> Alternatively, women could rise through the ranks through ruthlessness and prowess in combat. Leadership roles, especially for women, often came at a tremendous personal cost. Success frequently depended on using their bodies for survival and dominance, with many cultivating fear to avoid being seen as weak. Karina, for example, became one of FARC's most feared commanders through her battle injuries—such as losing an eye—and her reputation of brutality, making her one of the highest-ranking guerrillas in the group.<ref name=":11"/>

Despite these challenges, women in the FARC received political education and public speaking training, opportunities rarely available to women in the broader Colombian society.<ref name=":6"/>

==== Regulations of relationships and motherhood ====
Furthermore, FARC sought to control sexual relationships between combatants, requiring commander approval for romantic pairings. This was intended to reduce disruptions to combat readiness and organizational cohesion.<ref name=":8" /> Female combatants were also forced to use contraception.<ref name=":5"/> Some girls, even aged 12 years old, had an intrauterine device (IUD) inserted.<ref name=":7"/> The organization also maintained strict rules about pregnancy, often forcing or coercing abortions or requiring newborns to be given away to other families. Leaders decided that motherhood was incompatible with guerilla life, fearing it would reduce the woman's effectiveness as a combatant and risk the lives of both the mother and the child.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Alarcon |first=Luis |date=April 2019 |title=Role and Status of FARC's Women in the Colombian Conflict and in the Post Conflict |url=https://www.jetir.org/papers/JETIR1904945.pdf |journal=Journal of Emerging Technologies and Innovative Research |volume=6 |issue=4 |pages=298–299 |issn=2349-5162}}</ref>

== Human rights violations ==
{{Multiple image
| align = right
| direction = vertical
| width = 200
| image1 = Carro bomba Caracol Radio 20100812.jpg
| caption1 = A 12 August 2010 terrorist attack by the FARC with a car bomb at the headquarters of [[Caracol Radio]] left 43 people injured.
| image2 = 2012 car bombing in bogota colombia.JPG
| caption2 = 2012 car bombing targeting the former minister [[Fernando Londoño]]
}}
FARC was accused of committing violations of human rights by numerous groups, including Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International, the United Nations as well as by the Colombian, U.S. and European Union governments.

A February 2005 report from the United Nations' [[High Commissioner for Human Rights]] mentioned that, during 2004, "FARC–EP continued to commit grave breaches [of human rights] such as murders of protected persons, torture and hostage-taking, which affected many civilians, including men, women, returnees, boys and girls, and ethnic groups."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.hchr.org.co/documentoseinformes/informes/altocomisionado/Informe2004_eng.pdf |title=Report of the High Commissioner for Human Rights on the situation of human rights in Colombia |date=28 February 2005 |website=UN Commission on Human Rights |access-date=1 September 2006 |archive-date=19 April 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070419124731/http://www.hchr.org.co/documentoseinformes/informes/altocomisionado/Informe2004_eng.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>
<!--

=== Sexual abuse and forced abortions ===
According to [[Amnesty International]] it has been reported that young female recruits were sexually abused by veteran guerrilla soldiers and in several cases pregnancies were aborted against their will by FARC doctors.<ref name="amnesty.org">{{cite web |url=https://www.amnesty.org/en/documents/amr23/040/2004/en/ |title=Colombia: "Scarred bodies, hidden crimes": Sexual Violence against women in the armed conflict |date=12 October 2004 |website=Amnesty International |access-date=2012-10-14}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |url=http://www.foreignaffairs.com/articles/137672/anne-phillips/fighting-mad?page=show |title=Fighting Mad: Why Women Turn to the FARC - and How the FARC Turns on Them |first=Christine |last=Balling |date=June 1, 2012 |magazine=[[Foreign Affairs]] |access-date=2012-10-14}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.americas-forum.com/why-women-turn-to-the-farc-and-how-the-farc-turns-on-them/ |title=FP: Why Women Turn to the FARC — and How the FARC Turns on Them |first=Anne |last=Phillips |date=June 4, 2012 |website=Americas Forum |access-date=2012-10-14 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140222024447/http://www.americas-forum.com/why-women-turn-to-the-farc-and-how-the-farc-turns-on-them/ |archive-date=22 February 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2008/aug/24/farc.colombia |work=The Guardian |first=Alice |last=O'Keeffe |title=Jungle fever: Alice O'Keeffe meets the women from FARC's female troops who have given up the revolution |date=24 August 2008 |location=London}}</ref>

=== Child soldiers ===
FARC–EP, the ELN and right-wing paramilitaries all trained teens as soldiers and informants. [[Human Rights Watch]] estimates that the FARC-EP had the majority of [[Military use of children|child combatants]] in Colombia, and that approximately one quarter of its guerrillas were under 18.<ref name="hrw-learn-not-to-cry">{{cite report |url=https://www.hrw.org/reports/2003/colombia0903/colombia0903.pdf |title='You'll Learn Not to Cry': Child Combatants in Colombia |date=September 2003 |publisher=[[Human Rights Watch]] |isbn=1-56432-288-2 |access-date=1 September 2006}}</ref><ref name="Children">{{cite web |url=https://hrw.org/english/docs/2005/02/22/colomb10202.htm |title=Colombia: Armed Groups Send Children to War |date=22 February 2005 |website=Human Rights Watch |access-date=1 September 2006}}</ref> Forcible recruitment of children, by either side, was rare in Colombia. They joined for a variety of reasons including poverty, lack of educational opportunities, avoiding dangerous work in coca processing, escaping from domestic violence, offers of money (mostly from paramilitaries, who pay their soldiers).<ref name="hrw-learn-not-to-cry"/> Human Rights Watch noted that "once integrated into the FARC-EP, children are typically barred from leaving".<ref name="HRW-2001-FARC-Recommendations">{{cite web |url=https://www.hrw.org/reports/2001/farc/Formatted%20FARC-Eng%208-241.htm#P52_1119 |title=International Humanitarian Law and its Application to the Conduct of the FARC-EP. – I. Summary and Recommendations |date=August 2001 |website=Human Rights Watch |access-date=20 August 2010}}</ref>

FARC-EP Commander [[Simón Trinidad]] has stated that FARC did not allow the enlistment of people under 15 years of age, arguing that this is in accordance with Article 38 of the United Nations' [[Convention on the Rights of the Child]].<ref name="beyond-bogota-57">{{cite book |title=Beyond Bogota: Diary of a Drug War Journalist in Colombia |first=Garry |last=Leech |publisher=Beacon Press |year=2009 |isbn=978-0-8070-6145-9 |url=https://archive.org/details/beyondbogotadiar00leec |url-access=registration |page=[https://archive.org/details/beyondbogotadiar00leec/page/57 57]}}; See also: Article 38 of [http://www2.ohchr.org/english/law/crc.htm UN Convention on the Rights of the Child] {{Webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100611182141/http://www2.ohchr.org/english/law/crc.htm |date=11 June 2010}}</ref> He also argued that the alternatives for many children in Colombia are worse, including prostitution and exploitative work in mines and coca production.<ref name="beyond-bogota-57"/><ref>{{cite news |title=Interview with FARC Commander Simón Trinidad |first=Garry |last=Leech |work=Colombia Journal |date=25 June 2000 |url=http://colombiajournal.org/colombia15.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140111210141/http://colombiajournal.org/colombia15.htm |archive-date=11 January 2014}}</ref> [[Amnesty International]] has rejected the validity of such a position in international law.<ref name="AMNESTY-Marulanda-2002"/>

In June 2000, FARC-EP Commander [[Carlos Antonio Lozada]] told Human Rights Watch that the minimum recruitment age of fifteen years was set in 1996 but admitted that "this norm was not enforced" until recently. Lozada said, however, that it had become an obligatory standard after Commander [[Jorge Briceño]]'s statements on the matter in April 2000.<ref name="HRW-2001-FARC-Child Soldiers">{{cite web |url=https://www.hrw.org/reports/2001/farc/Formatted%20FARC-Eng%208-241-07.htm#P326_50657 |title=International Humanitarian Law and its Application to the Conduct of the FARC-EP - VII. Child Soldiers |date=August 2001 |website=Human Rights Watch |access-date=20 August 2010}}</ref> A 2001 Human Rights Watch report considered FARC-EP's refusal to admit children under fifteen years old into their forces to be "encouraging" but added that there is "little evidence that this rule is being strictly applied" and called on the group to demobilize all existing child soldiers and cease this practice in the future.<ref name="HRW-2001-FARC-Recommendations"/>

In 2003, Human Rights Watch reported that FARC-EP showed no leniency to children because of their age, assigning minors the same duties as adults and sometimes requiring them to participate in executions or witness torture.<ref name="hrw-learn-not-to-cry"/>.-->

=== Extrajudicial executions ===
FARC consistently carried out attacks against civilians specifically targeting suspected supporters of paramilitary groups, political adversaries, journalists, local leaders, and members of certain indigenous groups since at least as early as 1994.<ref name="ucdp.uu.se">{{cite web |url=http://www.ucdp.uu.se/gpdatabase/gpcountry.php?id=35&regionSelect=5-Southern_Americas# |title=Colombia, One-Sided violence, FARC-Civilians, 1994–2010 |website=[[Uppsala Conflict Data Program]] Conflict Encyclopedia |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130606082744/http://www.ucdp.uu.se/gpdatabase/gpcountry.php?id=35&regionSelect=5-Southern_Americas |archive-date=6 June 2013}}</ref> From 1994 to 1997 the region of [[Urabá Antioquia|Urabá]] in [[Antioquia Department]] was the site of FARC attacks against civilians.<ref name="ucdp.uu.se"/> FARC has also executed civilians for failing to pay "war taxes" to their group.<ref name="ucdp.uu.se"/>

In 2001, [[Human Rights Watch]] (HRW) announced that the FARC–EP had abducted and executed civilians accused of supporting paramilitary groups in the [[El Caguán DMZ|demilitarized zone]] and elsewhere, without providing any legal defense mechanisms to the suspects and generally refusing to give any information to relatives of the victims. The human rights NGO directly investigated three such cases and received additional information about over twenty possible executions during a visit to the zone.<ref name="HRW-2001-FARC-ABDUCTIONSEXECUTIONS">{{cite web |url=https://www.hrw.org/reports/2001/farc/Formatted%20FARC-Eng%208-241-02.htm#P155_22204 |title=International Humanitarian Law and its Application to the Conduct of the FARC-EP. – III. Abductions and Extrajudicial Executions |work=[[Human Rights Watch]] |date=August 2001 |access-date=4 December 2016 |archive-date=18 March 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170318173526/https://www.hrw.org/reports/2001/farc/Formatted%20FARC-Eng%208-241-02.htm#P155_22204 |url-status=live }}</ref>

According to HRW, those extrajudicial executions would qualify as [[forced disappearances]] if they had been carried out by agents of the government or on its behalf, but nevertheless remained "blatant violations of the FARC–EP's obligations under international humanitarian law and in particular key provisions of article 4 of Protocol II, which protects against violence to the life, physical, and mental well-being of persons, torture, and ill-treatment".<ref name="HRW-2001-FARC-ABDUCTIONSEXECUTIONS"/>

The Colombian human rights organization CINEP reported that FARC–EP killed an estimated total of 496 civilians during 2000.<ref name="HRW-2001-FARC-ABDUCTIONSEXECUTIONS"/>

=== Use of gas cylinder mortars and land mines ===
The FARC–EP has employed a type of improvised [[mortar (weapon)|mortars]] made from gas canisters (or cylinders), when launching attacks.

According to [[Human Rights Watch]], the FARC–EP has killed civilians not involved in the conflict through the use of gas cylinder mortars<ref name="hrw">{{cite web |url=https://www.hrw.org/en/news/2005/04/15/colombia-more-farc-killings-gas-cylinder-bombs |title=More FARC Killings with Gas Cylinder Bombs: Atrocities Target Indigenous Group |date=25 April 2005 |website=Human Rights Watch |access-date=1 September 2006 |archive-date=16 January 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090116041915/http://www.hrw.org/en/news/2005/04/15/colombia-more-farc-killings-gas-cylinder-bombs |url-status=live }}</ref> and its use of [[land mine]]s.<ref name="wp20070726">{{cite news |first=Juan |last=Forero |title=Report Cites Rebels' Wide Use of Mines in Colombia |newspaper=The Washington Post |date=26 July 2007 |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2007/07/25/AR2007072501093.html?nav=rss_world/southamerica |access-date=13 February 2008 |page=A16 |archive-date=9 November 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121109164312/http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2007/07/25/AR2007072501093.html?nav=rss_world/southamerica |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[Human Rights Watch]] considers that "the FARC–EP's continued use of gas cylinder mortars shows this armed group's flagrant disregard for lives of civilians...gas cylinder bombs are impossible to aim with accuracy and, as a result, frequently strike civilian objects and cause avoidable civilian casualties."<ref name="hrw"/>

According to the [[ICBL]] Landmine and Cluster Munitions Monitor, "FARC is probably the most prolific current user of antipersonnel mines among rebel groups anywhere in the world." Furthermore, FARC use child soldiers to carry and deploy antipersonnel mines.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.the-monitor.org/index.php/publications/display?act=submit&pqs_year=2009&pqs_type=lm&pqs_report=colombia&pqs_section= |title=Colombia: 2008 Key Data |work=Landmine and Cluster Munition Monitor |access-date=17 October 2011 |archive-date=20 July 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110720033419/http://www.the-monitor.org/index.php/publications/display?act=submit&pqs_year=2009&pqs_type=lm&pqs_report=colombia&pqs_section= |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=O’Neill|first=Jacqueline|title=Are Women the Key to Peace in Colombia?|url=https://foreignpolicy.com/2015/04/20/are-women-the-key-to-peace-in-colombia-farc-talks/|access-date=2021-12-06|website=Foreign Policy|date=20 April 2015|language=en-US|archive-date=6 December 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211206205046/https://foreignpolicy.com/2015/04/20/are-women-the-key-to-peace-in-colombia-farc-talks/|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Treatment of women ===
Female membership of the group is around 30 to 40 percent<ref>{{Cite web |last=O’Neill |first=Jacqueline |title=Are Women the Key to Peace in Colombia? |url=https://foreignpolicy.com/2015/04/20/are-women-the-key-to-peace-in-colombia-farc-talks/ |access-date=2022-10-12 |website=Foreign Policy |date=20 April 2015 |language=en-US |archive-date=6 December 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211206205046/https://foreignpolicy.com/2015/04/20/are-women-the-key-to-peace-in-colombia-farc-talks/ |url-status=live }}</ref> and while FARC's official policy forbids sexual assault of any kind, female members have experienced rape, sex slavery, and [[forced abortion]]s. In a 2011 Colombia Police report, 112 women had deserted FARC and reported instances of being forced to have sex with commanding officers which lead to the spread of sexually transmitted diseases as well as pregnancy. Members who became pregnant were forced to have abortions at any stage of gestation, with an estimated 80 to 90 percent of ex-FARC female members having had at least one abortion, some having up to four. The report also claims that girls as young as 13 were recruited by FARC to fill a quota of women because "The women are [considered] necessary to maintain the discipline of the FARC."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Heyden |first=Tom |date=2011-06-13 |title=FARC's female guerrillas submitted to sexual slavery: Police report |url=https://colombiareports.com/colombian-police-report-details-sexual-atrocities-within-farc/ |access-date=2022-10-12 |website=Colombia News {{!}} Colombia Reports |language=en-US |archive-date=12 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221012144344/https://colombiareports.com/amp/colombian-police-report-details-sexual-atrocities-within-farc/ |url-status=live }}</ref> In an interview with [[Reuters]], Claudia Roa, who joined FARC when she was 14, told how she was unknowingly given pills to induce birth when she was 8 months pregnant, after which her child was suffocated to death. According to Roa, many other women faced similar treatment, but those who became girlfriends to commanders were awarded special privileges, including the right to have children.<ref>{{Citation |title=&quot;Abortions forced on Colombia's female rebels&quot; |date=2013-09-26 |url=https://vimeo.com/75490631 |access-date=2022-10-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211206205045/https://vimeo.com/75490631 |archive-date=6 December 2021 |url-status=live}}</ref> One Colombian newspaper, after reviewing uncovered FARC documents and speaking with investigators, estimated that 1,000 forced abortions occur each year in FARC camps.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-04-11 |title=Así obligan a las mujeres a abortar en las Farc |url=https://www.elespectador.com/judicial/asi-obligan-a-las-mujeres-a-abortar-en-las-farc-article-401836/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211206205048/https://www.elespectador.com/judicial/asi-obligan-a-las-mujeres-a-abortar-en-las-farc-article-401836/ |archive-date=6 December 2021 |access-date=2022-10-12 |website=El Espectador |language=es}}</ref> In 2015, the Colombian attorney general opened an investigation into 150 cases of ex-FARC women being forced to terminate their pregnancies.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-12-11 |title=Colombia investigates forced abortions for female fighters in rebel ranks |url=http://www.theguardian.com/world/2015/dec/11/colombia-investigates-forced-abortions-farc-female-fighters-in-rebel-ranks |access-date=2022-10-12 |website=the Guardian |language=en}}</ref>

=== Violence against indigenous people ===
FARC sometimes threatened or assassinated indigenous Colombian leaders for attempting to prevent FARC incursions into their territory and resisting the forcible recruitment by FARC of indigenous youth. Between 1986 and 2001, FARC was responsible for 27 assassinations, 15 threats, and 14 other abuses of indigenous people in Antioquia Department.<ref name="murillo-col-us-74"/>
In March 1999 members of a local FARC contingent killed 3 indigenous rights activists, who were working with the U'Wa people to build a school for U'Wa children, and were fighting against encroachment of U'Wa territory by multinational oil corporations. The killings were almost universally condemned, and seriously harmed public perceptions of FARC.<ref name="murillo-col-us-74"/>

Members of indigenous groups have demanded the removal of military bases set up by the Colombian government and guerrilla encampments established by FARC in their territories, claiming that both the [[Colombian National Army]] and the FARC should respect indigenous autonomy and international humanitarian law.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.google.com/hostednews/epa/article/ALeqM5hcjyOYRTZS13urZy_whouPKUd9BA?docId=157311 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120523004305/http://www.google.com/hostednews/epa/article/ALeqM5hcjyOYRTZS13urZy_whouPKUd9BA?docId=157311 |url-status=dead |archive-date=23 May 2012 |title=Indígenas colombianos exigen al Ejército y a las FARC desmontar sus "bases militares" |date=20 July 2011 |work=[[European Pressphoto Agency]] |language=es |access-date=14 October 2012 |via=Google News}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.lapress.org/articles.asp?art=6526 |title=We are a peaceful army |first=Susan |last=Abad |date=1 December 2011 |work=Latinamerica Press |access-date=14 October 2012 |archive-date=3 August 2012 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120803131022/http://www.lapress.org/articles.asp?art=6526 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="colombiareports.com">{{cite web |url=http://colombiareports.com/colombia-news/news/17781-indigenous-colombians-demand-land-from-army-and-farc.html |title=Indigenous groups demand army, FARC remove bases |first=Stephen |last=Manker |date=21 July 2011 |website=Colombia Reports |access-date=2012-10-14 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110723100556/http://colombiareports.com/colombia-news/news/17781-indigenous-colombians-demand-land-from-army-and-farc.html |archive-date=23 July 2011}}</ref> According to a 2012 research from the [[National Indigenous Organization of Colombia]] (ONIC), 80,000 members of indigenous communities have been displaced from their native lands since 2004 because of FARC-related violence.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.infosurhoy.com/cocoon/saii/xhtml/en_GB/features/saii/features/main/2011/12/05/feature-01 |title=FARC harasses indigenous Colombians |first=Carlos Andrés |last=Barahona |date=12 May 2011 |website=Infosur Hoy |access-date=2012-10-14 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120709211343/http://www.infosurhoy.com/cocoon/saii/xhtml/en_GB/features/saii/features/main/2011/12/05/feature-01 |archive-date=9 July 2012}}</ref> Luis Evelis, an indigenous leader and ONIC representative, has stated that "the armed conflict is still in force, causing damages to the indigenous. Our territories are self-governed and we demand our [[autonomy]]. During the year 2011, fifty-six indigenous people have been killed."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.dailymotion.com/video/xjuffm_atentados-ratifican-conflicto-en-colombia-activista_new |title=Atentados ratifican conflicto en Colombia (activista) |website=Vìdeo Dailymotion |date=11 July 2011 |language=es |access-date=2012-10-14 |archive-date=22 June 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120622012559/http://www.dailymotion.com/video/xjuffm_atentados-ratifican-conflicto-en-colombia-activista_new |url-status=live }}</ref> The [[United Nations]] [[Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples]] has indicated that no military activities may be carried out within indigenous territories without first undertaking an "effective consultation" with indigenous representatives and authorities from the communities involved.<ref name="colombiareports.com"/><ref name="democracyinaction">{{cite web |url=http://salsa.democracyinaction.org/o/967/t/0/blastContent.jsp?email_blast_KEY=1220543 |title=Mining Firm Agrees to Pay Compensation to Peruvian Farmers |date=21 July 2011 |work=[[Center for Economic and Policy Research]] |access-date=11 January 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131228101751/http://salsa.democracyinaction.org/o/967/t/0/blastContent.jsp?email_blast_KEY=1220543 |archive-date=28 December 2013}}</ref>

The Regional Indigenous Council of [[Cauca Department|Cauca]] (CRIC) issued a statement concerning the release of two hostages taken by FARC in 2011: "Compared to past statements made by the national government, it is important to reiterate that the presence of armed groups in our territories is a fact that has been imposed by force of arms, against which our communities and their leaders have remained in peaceful resistance." The CRIC also indicated that neither the Colombian government nor the mediators and armed groups involved consulted with the indigenous people and their authorities about the hostage release, raising concerns about the application of national and international law guaranteeing their autonomy, [[self-determination]] and self-government. The indigenous organization also demanded the immediate end of all violence and conflict within indigenous territories and called for a negotiated solution to the war.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://indigenouspeoplesissues.com/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=9007:colombia-statement-concerning-release-of-two-indigenous-hostages-by-farc&catid=23:south-america-indigenous-peoples&Itemid=56 |title=Colombia: Statement Concerning Release of Two Indigenous Hostages By FARC |date=2011-02-18 |website=Indigenous Peoples Issues and Resources |access-date=2012-10-14 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130502051837/http://indigenouspeoplesissues.com/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=9007%3Acolombia-statement-concerning-release-of-two-indigenous-hostages-by-farc&catid=23%3Asouth-america-indigenous-peoples&Itemid=56 |archive-date=2 May 2013}}</ref>

Official Colombian government statistics show that murders of indigenous people between January and May 2011 have increased 38% compared to the same timeframe in 2010.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.derechoshumanos.gov.co/Observatorio/Paginas/Observatorio.aspx |title=Observatorio de Derechos Humanos y Derecho Internacional Humanitario |website=Consejería Derechos Humanos |language=es |access-date=2012-10-14 |archive-date=24 April 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120424114031/http://www.derechoshumanos.gov.co/Observatorio/Paginas/Observatorio.aspx |url-status=dead }}</ref> Colombia is home to nearly 1&nbsp;million indigenous people, divided into around 100 different ethnicities.
